<meta>This page provides the official ecclesiastical approval for the book, following the "To the Reader" preface that concluded on page xxiij. This "Approbation" was a standard requirement in 17th-century France to ensure that religious works were doctrinally sound and free from heresy.</meta>

### Approval of the Doctors.

<note>In the 17th century, "Doctors" refers specifically to Doctors of Theology—experts authorized by the Church or the University to vet manuscripts before they were granted a license to be printed.</note>

Monsieur Corneille <note>Pierre Corneille (1606–1684), the celebrated French dramatist known for *Le Cid*, who spent several years translating this work into French verse.</note> having successfully completed this admirable translation of the book of the *Imitation of Jesus Christ*, we are obliged to offer this final testimony to the truth in its favor: that it could not have been better done, and that everything within it is Catholic, Orthodox, and in accordance with the author's meaning. We do not doubt that such an excellent work, where Poetry speaks the language of the Saints so purely, will find the approval it deserves, and that the Charity which has supplied its richest ideas will warm the hearts of those who have the piety to read it with focus. Given at Rouen <note>Corneille’s birthplace and a major center for French publishing at the time.</note> on this day of Saint Matthias, the twenty-fifth of February, one thousand six hundred and fifty-six.

->*Signed*,<-

->Gaulde, and R. le Cornier.<-

### CHAPTER I.

*Of the Imitation of Jesus Christ, and of the contempt of all the <term>vanities<note>In this spiritual context, "vanities" refers to the emptiness or worthlessness of worldly pursuits compared to eternal life.</note></term> of the World.*

Happy is he who keeps to the path where my voice invites him;
Darkness never approaches him who follows me,
And everywhere in my footsteps he finds a day without night,
Which carries the light of life into the very heart.
Thus speaks Jesus Christ; thus the rays of his virtues—
With which the paths he trod for us shine—
Show, by their ever-vivid beams, how one must live;

<meta>This page continues the poetic French translation of Book One, Chapter I of "The Imitation of Christ." It follows the opening quatrain and focuses on the necessity of the Holy Spirit to understand Christ's teachings, contrasting intellectual pride with humble devotion.</meta>

# THE IMITATION OF

And whoever desires to be fully enlightened,
Must learn from him, that it is only by following him,
That the heart is freed from all blindness.

The doctrines of the Saints have nothing that compares
To that of which he himself has made the mirror;
It holds a thousand treasures, which soon reveal themselves,
When the eye has his adorable spirit for a torch.
You, who are attached to yourself by self-love,
Listen to and read [his word] without being moved;
For lack of this spirit, you find only thorns there.
But if you wish to understand and read with pleasure,
Conform your life to it, and its divine sweetnesses
Will spread in abundance toward your happy desire.

What does it profit you to pierce the most secret abysses
Where the immense Trinity <note>The Christian doctrine of God as three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> hides from our senses,
If your inner self, lacking humility,
Cannot offer him pleasing sacrifices?
This proud knowledge, these pompous sentiments
Are but vain ornaments in the eyes of God;
He does not stoop toward such haughty souls;
And virtue without them is of such value,
That it is better to truly feel the sorrow of your sins,
Than to be able to define what that sorrow is.

Carry the whole Bible imprinted in your memory,
Know all that the Sages of olden times have said;
Add to it, if you can, all the striking events
Of secular history <note>original: *Histoire profane*; refers to worldly or non-religious history.</note> and of sacred history;
From so many teachings, the powerless languor
Under their useless weight will overwhelm your heart,
If God does not also pour his love and grace therein:

### JESUS CHRIST. Book I.
->A 2<-

This is the profound wisdom of the truly Wise,
It is good at all times, it is good in all places,
And the surest path to reach the Heavens
Is to steady our steps upon the contempt of the World. <note>original: *mépris du Monde*; a reference to the medieval ascetic concept of *contemptus mundi*, which suggests prioritizing spiritual life over material distractions.</note>
This dangerous flatterer of our weak minds
Opposes a thousand attractions to this just contempt;
Whoever allows themselves to be dazzled is soon seduced:
But open your eyes wide to their fragility,
See that a single moment suffices to destroy them,
And you will see that, in the end, all is but vanity. <note>In this context, "vanity" (from the Latin *vanitas*) refers to things that are empty, fleeting, or hollow, rather than just conceit.</note>

Vanity to heap riches upon riches,
Vanity to languish in the thirst for honors,
Vanity to choose as our highest happiness
The damnable caresses of the flesh and the senses:
Vanity to aspire to see our days last
Without being concerned with better regulating their course,
To love a long life, and neglect a good one,
To embrace the present without care for the future,
And to value a single moment that the world gives us
More than the expectation of goods that will never end.

You then, whoever you are, if you wish to understand well
How little you should trust your deceptive senses,
Remember that one can never satisfy
The human eye with seeing, nor the ear with hearing; <note>A paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 1:8, emphasizing that material experiences cannot fulfill the soul.</note>
That one must steal away from so many false charms,
To despise what is seen for what is not seen,
To flee the pleasures transmitted by these organs,
For there is no place to be truly satisfied by them,
And that attachment to their profane sweetnesses
Sullies your conscience, and distances you from God.

### CHAPTER II.

->*On the low esteem of oneself.*<-

The desire to know is natural to men,
It is born in their cradle and dies only with them;
But, O God, whose hand makes us what we are,
What can this desire bear that is fruitful without the fear of You? <note>In this context, "fear" refers to "filial fear"—a profound respect and awe for God that steers one away from wrongdoing, rather than cowering terror.</note>

A simple peasant, humble and without experience,
Who does nothing but love You and possesses only Faith,
Is worth more than a Philosopher puffed up with his science,
Who probes the Heavens without reflecting on himself. <note>original: *stupide*; in the 17th century, this term often meant "unlearned" or "simple" rather than "unintelligent." The "Philosopher" here refers to astronomers or scholars who study the physical laws of the universe while neglecting their own spiritual state.</note>

He who knows himself has a soul with little vanity,
His own self-knowledge makes him value himself very little;
And all the false brilliance of human praise
Is for him only an object of noble contempt.

On the great day of the Lord, will it be a great refuge
To have known the cause and effect of everything?
And will what one has known sway a Judge,
Who will look only at what one has done? <note>This reflects a core theme of the book: that on Judgment Day, moral actions and the state of the soul matter more than intellectual achievements.</note>

Limit your desires, then, to what you must do,
Do not carry them too far toward the heap of knowledge;
The cares of acquiring it do nothing but distract you,
And once you have acquired it, it can deceive you.

Scholars usually love to be looked at,
To have people whisper around them, "there go the great minds";
And if they do not keep a careful watch over their hearts,
They are always overtaken by this secret pride.

However, if it is true that there are some branches of learning <note>original: *sciences*; in the 17th century, this referred to any systematic body of knowledge, including theology and philosophy, rather than just the physical sciences.</note>

Your pride dares to prefer you to another;
See that there are yet more learned men in the world,
Whom Heaven deigns to enlighten even better.

Shun "high" science, and pursue the "good" kind;
Learn the art of living here below without worldly fame;

### CHAPTER IX.

#### *On obedience and subjection.*

How good it is to obey! What merit a man has,
Who loves to follow the laws of a Superior, <note>term: "Superior" (French: *Superieur*). In a monastic or religious context, this refers to the head of a religious house or an ecclesiastical authority to whom a monk or priest owes obedience.</note>

But it holds only bitterness without this charity, <note>In this context, "charity" refers to *Caritas*, or the selfless love of God, rather than simply giving to the poor.</note>

Who loves to follow the laws of a Superior, <note>term: "Superior" (French: *Superieur*). In a religious community, this is the person in charge, such as an abbot or mother superior, who represents divine authority.</note>

Finally encounter there only an imaginary good,
Whose deceptive idea vanishes in a moment.

It is true that everyone willingly counsels themselves,
That they love for their own sense <note>term: "sense" (French: *sens*). In this context, it refers to one's personal judgment, private opinion, or way of perceiving a situation.</note> to rule their actions,
And turn their inclinations with pleasure
Toward those whose thoughts are similar to their own;
But if the God of peace reigns at the bottom of our hearts,
We must tear them away from all these sweetnesses,
Suspect the weakness of all our sentiments,
Contradict them often, and to do so better,
Remember that on Earth there is no wise man
Who can conceive of everything without any error.

Do not then place such full confidence in your own thoughts
That you do not still open your ear to those of others;
And when you convince yourself that you judge better than another,
Sacrifice to your God this rightful belief.
To fight a revolt where reason leans, <note>This describes the internal struggle of a person who is logically correct but chooses to submit to another's will for the sake of humility.</note>
To give to good sense an unjust prison,
Is to do oneself a holy injustice;
And to achieve this, the more you have fought yourself,
The more this God, who looks upon such a great sacrifice,
Credits you with merit and advances you in virtue.

One walks with a firmer step in following than in leading;
Advice is easier to take than to give;
One can obey poorly, just as one can command poorly;
But it is much safer to listen than to instruct.
I know that man is free, and that his will,
Between two sentiments of equal goodness,
Can embrace one or the other with equal fruit;
But to never defer to that of one's neighbor,
When order or reason speaks against our—
-> own, <-
Is to show a stubborn or vain spirit.

### CHAPTER X.
#### *That one must avoid the superfluity of words.*

Flee the world’s entanglements as much as you can,
These worldly conversations <note>original: "entretiens du Siécle". In this context, "Siécle" (the Century) refers to the secular world and its distractions, as opposed to the cloistered or spiritual life.</note> have too much vanity;
And peace encounters an invincible obstacle there,
Even when one joins in with simplicity.

Suddenly the soul is defiled, and the heart made a slave
To the vain amusements they know how to give us;
Their force is marvelous, and for one who braves them,
A thousand let themselves be chained by their false charms.

Their flattering lure has the art of surprising us,
The poison it slips in is immediately poured;
And I would often wish to have been unable to hear anything,
Or to have seen no one, or not to have spoken at all.

What then gives birth in us to this senseless ardor,
This desire to speak spread everywhere,
If it is so difficult for the soul to re-enter itself
Without being wounded after this lost time?

Is it not that each one, incapable of helping themselves,
Hopes for mutual help from another;
And that the spirit, weary of the care that overwhelms it,
Seeks to evaporate it, at least in speech?

At least all these discourses upon which man throws himself,
His own interest alone forms and conducts them;
He speaks with pleasure of everything he desires,
He speaks with sorrow of everything that harms him.

But often it is in vain, and this false joy

Those spiritual riches by which the soul is enriched,
Places a poor guard upon our tongue,
And creates this long-standing abuse under which man grows old. <note>original: "blanchit". Literally "whitens," referring to the hair turning white with age while a person remains stuck in the same bad habits of idle talk.</note>

Let us speak, then, but in humble and holy conversation,
Which can help us acquire this kind of wealth;
God always pours it out beyond all hope,
When we unite in Him for such discussions.

### CHAPTER XI.
#### *That one must strive to acquire interior peace, and progress in the spiritual life.*

How much peace we would have, and how strong it would be,
If we only set our heart on what concerns us,
And if we did not love to trouble our spirits
With either what is done or what is said!
How could peace reign in him who, without ceasing,
Is anxious and busied with the affairs of others,
Who seeks outside of himself for things to worry him,
And rarely tries to collect himself within?

It is you, the simple-hearted, it is you whose happy prudence...

[He who avoids external distractions]
Possesses an abundance of true peace of mind;
It is through this that the Saints—dead to all those pleasures
Where earthly cares degrade our desires—
Having their hearts set only on God, and their eyes only on themselves,
Raised both to the supreme Truths;
And by limiting their actions to contemplating them,
They attained the highest level of perfection.

As for us, enslaved to our base desires,
We occupy our lives with fleeting goods;
And our spirit throws itself greedily
Wherever it is cast by their empty allure.

It is also rare that we have the glory
Of winning a full victory over even a single vice;
Our meager courage is suddenly beaten down,
And we poorly tend the fire that virtue kindles;
And far from striving to ensure such a beautiful heat
Gains new strength day by day,
We allow its weak ardor to grow lukewarm,
Until it degenerates from tepidity into coldness.

If the soul, purified of so many distractions,
Were perfectly mortified <note>original: "mortifiée". In this spiritual context, mortification refers to the "killing off" of selfish desires and the mastery of the physical senses to allow the spirit to focus entirely on the divine.</note> within itself,
It could then—as Queen of the senses—
Direct piercing eyes even to the throne of God,
And have a peaceful and holy <note>The OCR reads "ponte," likely a misreading of the 17th-century "sainte" (holy).</note> experience
Of the sweetness that His hand pours into the conscience.
But the empire of the senses presents other objects;
The soul serves as a slave to its own subjects.
We disdain to enter the perfect path
That the fervor of the Saints cleared with joy;
The slightest blow of adversity
Triumphs in a moment over our cowardice,
And makes us turn—blind as we are—
To the consolations offered by men.

But since we find even greater difficulty
In fully taming our own will;
If you cannot master yourself in small matters,
Tell me, when will you overcome yourself in great ones?

Resist your inclinations from the very beginning,

And strip away your bad habits entirely;

Silently builds an even greater obstacle.

Finally, set your life in order, and see—if you change—
What peace dwells within you, and what joy for the Angels!
Ah, if you could only see it, you would be more constant
In running without rest toward the happiness that awaits you!
You would take greater care to nourish in your soul
The holy and living ardor of a celestial flame; <note>The "celestial flame" refers to the fire of divine love or "charity," a central concept in Christian mysticism where the soul is purified by the heat of devotion.</note>
And by striving to increase it at every hour, in every place,
Each moment of your days would be a step toward God.

### CHAPTER XII.

->*On the benefits of adversity.*<-

It is good sometimes to feel setbacks, <note>original: "traverses". In this context, it refers to the "crosses" or hardships that block one's path or desires.</note>
And to experience their harshness;
They call a man back to the center of his heart,
And paint before his eyes his various miseries:
They make him see clearly
That he is but in exile in this World, <note>In 17th-century spiritual thought, "exile" refers to the belief that the soul's true home is in Heaven, and earthly life is a temporary, often difficult, period of separation.</note>
And through a sudden distaste, they prevent him from placing
Either his love or his hope within it.

It is advantageous that people blame and censure
Our most sincere actions;

### CHAPTER XVI.

*How one must bear the faults of others.*

Bear with patience in every other, and in yourself,
->What you cannot correct there;<-
Until the supreme power of God
Orders it otherwise, and deigns to change it.

To test your strength, it is perhaps better
->That He allows this cross to endure:<- <note>In this context, a "cross" is any personal trial, burden, or difficult person that serves as a spiritual exercise.</note>
Your merit will thereby be better known,
And if it is not put to the test, it is of no great weight.

You must, however, lift your prayer to Heaven
->Against such a long hindrance,<-
So that His goodness may grant you full grace regarding it,
Or help you to suffer it a little more gently.

### CHAPTER XVII.

->*Of the Monastic Life.*<-

**B**ecome highly skilled in the art of self-restraint,
Of stifling your desires, of breaking your own wishes,
If you desire a firm peace with everyone,
If you wish to remove from them any reason to complain.
To live in community without quarrel and without noise,
To carry until death a heart truly humbled <note>original: "reduit." In this spiritual context, it refers to a heart that has been brought low or subdued in humility before God.</note>,
->This is to make oneself worthy of envy:<-
Thrice happy is the one who makes such a lot for themselves,
Thrice happy is the one whom such a sweet life
->Leads toward a happy death.<-

If you wish to be worthy, if you wish to grow in grace,
Consider yourself here below only as a traveler, an exile;
Appear foolish for your God <note>A reference to the "fools for Christ" mentioned in 1 Corinthians 4:10—those who reject worldly status for the sake of the Gospel.</note>, take up this infinite zeal
Which pursues shame <note>original: "l'oprobre." This refers to the worldly disgrace or reproach often faced by the devout.</note>, and never tires of it.
The tonsure <term>tonsure: the practice of shaving the top of the scalp as a sign of religious devotion and humility</term> and the habit <term>habit: the distinctive clothing worn by members of a religious order</term> provide some outward appearance;
But do not assume that the hardships of the body
->Make a soul religious:<-
It is in the detachment from your earthly affections
That, in the midst of a harsh and laborious life,
->True religious duties consist.<-

Seek God, seek in Him the salvation of your soul,
Without seeking anything else under this pretense;
You will encounter only bitterness and pain,
If ever within your Cloister <note>original: "Cloître." Literally a covered walkway in a monastery, here used to represent the monastic life or the institution itself.</note> another desire inflames you.
Strive to be the least and the servant of all;
Or that peace of mind which seems so sweet to you,
->Will hardly be within your power:<-

### CHAPTER XIX.
*On the Exercises of the Good Monk.* <note>The French "Religieux" refers to any person—monk, friar, or nun—living under a religious rule.</note>

You who have enclosed your life within a <term>Cloister</term> <note>A cloister is the secluded living quarters of a monastery; here it symbolizes the entire life of religious separation from the world.</note>, strive to enrich it with every virtue; it is in this worthy effort that you should grow old <note>The original French "blanchir" (to whiten) refers to hair turning white over a long life of service.</note>. Your <term>Rule</term> <note>The "Rule" is the specific code of conduct for a religious order, such as the Rule of Saint Benedict.</note> teaches it to you, and your <term>habit</term> <note>The distinctive clothing of a religious order, such as a robe or cowl.</note> invites you to it. Through a holy gathering of these living treasures, ensure that your internal spirit matches the outward display, so that you are before God just as you appear before men. Indeed, take all the more care of the interior, because God is never deceived in knowing who we are, and He stands as witness to the depths of the heart.

Our respect owes Him praise in all places; He sees us everywhere, and He judges us everywhere. And as we walk everywhere before His eyes, we must carry the purity of the Angels with us everywhere. Each day, begin again by giving Him your heart; renew your <term>vows</term>, rekindle your fervor, and persist in saying to Him while asking for His Grace:
> Help me, Lord, and serve as a support
> To the good beginnings that I embrace under Your laws;
> For until now, what I have done is nothing. <note>This reflects a core principle of the *Imitation*: the "perpetual beginner" who never assumes they have achieved spiritual perfection.</note>

In the journey toward Heaven, the soul of the righteous man advances only as much as his resolve increases in firmness. His progress, which depends on constant effort, requires great diligence to produce great fruit. For if even the most constant and steadfast man often wavers, or often falls halfway, and is never so strong as to be unshakable; what shall become of those whose hearts are languishing and...

No matter how much an exile he is, or what perils he sees,
Loves to see himself charmed by false sweetness!
Ah, if he can allow such a cheer
-> To keep his senses in full bloom, <-
He does not see how quickly it flees; and his own weakness,
-> Which he takes as his mistress, <-
Hides his true misery from his dazzled eyes.

Yes, his levity, which every desire sets aflame,
And the little care he takes for his own failings,
Having rendered him <term>insensible</term><note>original: "stupide." In the 17th century, this term often meant "numb" or "dull to the senses" rather than a lack of intelligence.</note> to the interests of the soul,
Do not allow him to feel its many ills:
Thus, however great they may be, he never
-> Sighs for them, <-
-> For lack of considering them; <-
The more he is wounded by them, the more he admires himself,
-> And often dares to laugh <-
When from every side he has cause to weep.

Man, learn that there is no true
-> Liberty, <-
Nor any perfect pleasure, except in the fear of God;
And that the conscience, without stain or wound,
Can alone give place to such treasures:
All other liberty is but a long slavery

### CHAPTER XXII.
*Of the consolations of human misery.*

Mortal, open your eyes, and see that misery
->Seeks you out, and follows you everywhere;<-
And that all life is a bitter spring
->Unless it turns toward God.<-

Nothing should disturb you, nothing should surprise you,
->When the outcome fails your desires,<-
Since your fate is such that you should expect from it
->Only subjects of displeasure.<-

Do not hope that here it will ever lower itself
->To answer all your wishes;<-
For you, for me, for all, the rule is general,
->And never slackens.<-

There is no office, nor rank whose greatness is shielded
->From this inevitable law;<-
And those seen carrying the Sceptre, or the <term>Tiara</term><note>The Sceptre represents kings (secular power), while the Tiara refers to the Pope (religious power). The poet emphasizes that even the highest authorities are subject to human suffering.</note>,
->Are no more exempt from it than you.<-

Anguish enters everywhere, and if anyone on Earth
->Bears this common sorrow better;<-
It is he who for God knows how to <term>wage war against himself</term><note>This refers to the concept of "spiritual warfare," where a believer fights against their own ego, desires, and vices to remain faithful.</note>,
->And takes pleasure in suffering for Him.<-

The weak, however, say with envy,
->See how powerful this man is;<-

### CHAPTER XXIII.

->*On the Meditation on Death.*<-

Think, Mortal, and resolve yourself to this:
It will soon be over with you.
He who today gives the law
Is tomorrow reduced to dust.
The day that appears the most beautiful
Often casts into the grave
The memory most firmly established;
And the object one loves the best
Soon escapes the mind,
Once it is no longer before the eyes.

Yet your <term>dulled soul</term> <note>original: "ame ſtupide". In this historical context, "stupid" refers to a soul that is numbed, senseless, or paralyzed to spiritual things because it is overwhelmed by physical senses.</note>,
Over which the senses have all power,
Wishes to see nothing in the future
That might charm or intimidate it.
A fatal drowsiness
In your heart, which the soul poorly lights,
Permits no holy flame,

If you cannot do so today,
Will tomorrow be any less difficult?
Do you hold time in your own hand,
Or see any certainty
That you will even reach that tomorrow?

### CHAPTER XXIV.

#### *Of Judgment, and the punishments of sin.*

Man, whatever you wish to undertake here below,
Think of that exact account <note>Original: *conte exact*. This refers to the "reckoning" or spiritual audit of one's life that Christian tradition says occurs after death.</note> that one day must be rendered,
And set before your eyes this final end
Which will be your ill-fated, or your happy destiny.
Look with what face you will be able to appear
Before the Tribunal of your sovereign Master,
Before this just Judge from whom nothing is hidden,
Who reads your sin even within your heart,
Whom no gift dazzles, whom no error deceives,
Who is never surprised by the cleverness of an excuse,
Who renders justice to all, and weighs with the same weight
What Shepherds <note>Original: *Bergers*. Here used to represent the common or poorest people, illustrating that God does not favor the powerful.</note> do, and what Kings do.

Wretched sinner, what will you know how to answer
To this God who knows everything, and will come to confound you,
You whom the fleeting wrath of a mortal like yourself
Often fills with an invincible terror?

Set your affairs in order for this great day,
For this great day—the height, or the end of miseries—
Where each one, too burdened by his own load,
His own accuser, and his own executioner <note>Original: *bourreau*. A vivid image suggesting that the sinner’s own conscience becomes the instrument of their punishment.</note>,
Will answer with his own mouth, and alone in his defense
Will have no help but that of his <term>penitence</term> <note>Original: *penitence*. In this 17th-century context, this refers to the Catholic practice of contrition, confession, and acts of reparation performed during life to prepare the soul for God.</note>.

<vocab>Judgment, sin, Tribunal, Judge, Shepherds, Kings, penitence</vocab>

<summary>This page introduces Chapter 24, focusing on the Final Judgment and the impartiality of divine justice. It warns the reader that neither social rank nor clever excuses will matter when the soul stands alone before God.</summary>

How far their narrow and faithful observance reaches.
They live retired, and seldom go out;
Coarsely clothed, and poorly fed,
They work without rest, as well as without murmur,
Speak little, sleep little, rise in the morning,
Prolong their prayer, <note>Original: "oraison." A formal or contemplative prayer.</note> prolong their reading,
And under these harsh laws meet a sweet end.

See these great squadrons of industrious souls,
See the Order of the Carthusians, <note>The Carthusians (Chartreux) are a silent, contemplative Catholic order founded by St. Bruno in 1084, known for their extreme austerity.</note> see that of the Cistercians, <note>The Cistercians (Cîteaux) are a monastic order focused on manual labor and self-sufficiency, following the Rule of St. Benedict.</note>

It would be shameful for you to show any slowness,
When on Earth such a great number of Angels <note>A poetic reference to monks and nuns, who were often described as living an "angelic life" because of their focus on perpetual worship.</note>

O, if we could only live and have nothing to do,
But to dissipate within us this shameful lethargy;
But to praise this great Master, both with mouth and heart,
Without anything lower becoming necessary to us!
O, if the Christian soul and its holiest transports
Were not enslaved to the weaknesses of the body,
To the needs of sleeping, eating, and drinking;
If nothing interrupted a continual care
To proclaim God’s kindness and glory,
And to advance the spirit in the spiritual realm!

How happy we would be! How a year, a day, an hour,
Would make us taste much more felicity, <note>Intense happiness or spiritual bliss.</note>
Than entire centuries of the captivity
To which the flesh reduces us in its sad dwelling!
O God! why must these infirmities,
These daily tributes, <note>A metaphor for the basic biological needs—food, sleep, etc.—that "tax" the soul's time.</note> be necessities

When a man masters himself, and when the creatures
Of this world have no sweetness that can hold him back,
It is then that he begins to taste, without effort,
How sweet the Creator is to pure souls:
Then, whatever may happen, whether of good or ill,
He lives always content, and with an unwavering countenance
He receives both bad and good fortune;
Abundance falls upon him without moving him,
Poverty is never a burden to him,
Glory and contempt have but the same power over him.

It is then that he rests entirely in God,
In God is his confidence, and his only support,
In God whom he sees everywhere—in himself, in others—
In God who, for his soul, is all in all things.
Wherever he may be, whatever he may do, he fears and cherishes
This universal Being in whom nothing perishes,
And in whom everything preserves an immortal life;
Who never knows the shifting of time,
And whose voice is followed so quickly by the effect,
That saying and doing are not, in Him, two separate moments.

You who, though mortal, inconstant, and miserable,
Can easily save yourself with His help,
Remember the end toward which you must arrive,
And that lost time can never be recovered.
Go, run, fly without ceasing to fruitful labors;

If your soul perseveres within a noble fire, <note>Original: "un beau feu." A metaphor for divine love or spiritual fervor.</note>
You shall no longer fear any fatal assault;

A soul that often gives in to minor faults

But perfect joy arrives with the evening
For those who have spent their day fruitfully.
Watch over yourself, then, and over your desires;

Regardless of others, never neglect yourself.
Constraint yourself, compel yourself, change from good to better;
For the more a heart does violence to itself to correct its ways, <note>A reference to the biblical idea that "the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence" (Matthew 11:12), meaning it requires intense spiritual effort.</note>

Humble simplicity flies straight to God;
Purity embraces Him, and the two joined together
Attach themselves to His goodness and taste it in every place.

No good action would be a burden to you,
If you detached yourself from all disordered ways;
The insolent disorder of one's own feelings <note>original: "propres sentiments." In this context, it refers to self-will, or allowing personal emotions and biases to override divine will.</note>
Forms the entire burden of human weakness.
Seek here only to please this great Sovereign, <note>The "Sovereign" refers to God.</note>
Seek only to serve your neighbor <term>neighbor: from the French "prochain," referring to any fellow human being whom one has a moral duty to help</term> after Him,
And you will see yourself free within your soul;
You will be above your own fragility,
And will no longer have a part in the infamous slavery
Where man is cast by all other cares.

If your heart were upright, all creatures <note>In 17th-century spiritual writing, "creatures" refers to all of God's handiwork, including animals, plants, and the physical world.</note>
Would be mirrors and open books to you,
Where you would see constantly in a thousand different places
Models for living and pure doctrines.
All of them, as if in competition, show you their Author; <note>The "Author" is a common title for the Creator.</note>
He has imprinted His greatness even in the lowest of things,
And in the smallest, He is even more admirable;
Nothing speaks of His full goodness only halfway,
And the terrifying mass of the vast elephant
Does not display it better than the smallest ant.

---

Purify the interior, make it good and without stain,
Then you will see everything without trouble or hindrance;
And you will know how to understand, both quickly and powerfully,
What the thick veil of the passions <term>passions: in this era, this word refers to uncontrolled emotions or worldly desires that cloud the intellect</term> hides from you.
To the clean and pure heart, the soul lends eyes
Which penetrate Hell and pierce to the Heavens;
It sees everything as it is, and is never deceived.
But the heart that is poorly purified has only the eyes of the body;
All its knowledge, like those eyes, is confused,
And as it is within, so it judges what is without.

Truly, if there is any solid joy to be found here,
It is this purified heart alone that can taste it;

It is in an impure heart that it enters and unfolds.

Takes on a bright color in the midst of the flame:
This is a true image of a full return toward God;
His fire dissipates the soul’s heaviness,
And makes of an old man <term>old man: a biblical reference to the unregenerate, sinful nature of humanity before spiritual renewal</term> a man who is entirely new.

When this fire cools, man suddenly fears
Even the smallest labor, even the slightest efforts;
And he suffers with pleasure the sweetness of outward things,
Regardless of the secret traps this pleasure sets for him:
But when he begins to triumph over himself,
When he chooses God as master, and as his only King,
When he walks with courage in His holy way;
The greatest labor can no longer exhaust him,
The more he does violence to himself, the more he finds relief, <note>This refers to the concept of "holy violence"—the spiritual struggle to overcome one's own ego and disordered desires.</note>
And that which once overwhelmed him ceases to weigh him down.

#### *Of the Familiar Friendship of JESUS CHRIST.*

Free yourself from slavery, and know how to purge yourself

### CHAPTER XI.

*Of the small number of those who love the Cross of JESUS CHRIST.*

How many men, in love with celestial glory,
View the Cross as a fatal burden,
And seek to taste its consolations,
Without wishing to experience its tribulations!
Jesus Christ sees this fickle temperament everywhere;
He has only too many friends to sit at His table,
None at the banquet wish to abandon Him,
But in the Desert <note>Refers to Christ’s forty days of fasting in the wilderness, symbolizing a time of spiritual trial and isolation.</note> He is alone in fasting:
All ask Him for a share in His full joy,
But none wish to take part in His full sorrow;
Those whose ardor seems the readiest to offer itself,
Leave Him first when He must suffer.

Up to the breaking of this bread <note>original: "la fraction de ce pain" — a reference to the Eucharist or the miraculous multiplication of loaves.</note> that He gives us,
Enough people follow and surround Him here;
But few allow their love to be so inflamed
As to drink with Him from the bitter cup. <term>bitter cup: original: "calice amer" — a reference to the "cup" of suffering Christ accepted in the Garden of Gethsemane before His crucifixion.</term>
The brilliant miracles with which He sows His life
Hardly kindle our desire with their brilliance,
Before His shameful death cools our spirits,
To the point of no longer wanting this gift at such a price.

Many love and bless Him with warmth,

Whose praises dry up at the first setback:
As long as they have no adversity to lament,
And He pours out only His kindness <note>original: "benignité" — refers to God's gracious benevolence or favor.</note> upon them,
This tangible favor easily serves as a lure
To sustain their zeal and preserve their strength;

A sudden ice deadens all that fire,
And the smoking remains of their extinguished fervor
Send forth from the heart nothing but murmurs and complaints,
While in the depths of the soul a cowardly astonishment
Turns firmness into despondency.

Do you act this way, you whose extreme love
Embraces Jesus Christ only for His own sake,
And who, without looking to your own interest,
Have no passion but for what pleases Him?
You see with the same eye all that He sends you;
You love Him in anguish as much as in joy;
You know how to bless Him in prosperity,
You know how to praise Him in calamity;
An equal constancy, following in His footsteps,
Finds reason to give Him thanks in either fate;
And even if He had nothing but rigors for you,
The same thanks would depart from your hearts.

Pure love of Jesus, how strange is your strength
When self-love <term>self-love: original: "amour propre" — in 17th-century spiritual writing, this refers to a disordered, ego-driven love of oneself that competes with the pure love of God.</term> makes no mixture within you,
And when, fully stripped of self-interest,
You are unstained by any backward glance toward yourself!
Do they not have a servile and mercenary love,
Those hearts that love God only to satisfy themselves,
And make Him the object of their affections
Only to receive consolations from Him?

To love God in such a way, and for our own benefit,
Is to unworthily put His goodness into our service for wages,
To believe that with a few prayers we pay for all His support,
And in the end to love ourselves more than Him.
But where will one find a soul so purified,
And to such a degree released from the hope of any reward,
That she loves to serve God without considering herself,
And seeks in loving Him only the joy of adoring Him?

Certainly, few are seen whose love is so pure
As to strip away every created thing;
And if there is on Earth one truly poor in spirit <note>original: "pauvre d'esprit" — a reference to the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3), implying a spiritual humility and total reliance on God rather than material or intellectual wealth.</note>,
Who, detached from everything, belongs entirely to Jesus Christ;
It is a treasure so great that those fertile mines
That Nature scatters at the ends of the New Worlds <note>A 17th-century reference to the Americas and the wealth (gold, silver) being extracted from them at the time.</note>,
Those seas where the pearl and the coral harden,
Have never conceived of anything of equal value.

But also, it is not an easy conquest
That man finds exposed to his first desires:
When to achieve it he gives all his wealth,
Even with this great effort, he has still done nothing;
Whatever harsh penance <term>penance: original: "penitence" — acts of self-mortification or discipline intended to show repentance for sin.</term> he imposes on himself here below,
His longest rigors are still of little consequence;
Though he applies his care to every science,
Though he possesses them entirely, he is still very far;
Though he has a thousand virtues, whose happy assembly
Adorns his great courage with all their ornaments;
Though his devotion, though his high fervors
Attract new favors every day;
Know that much still remains for him to do
If he fails in this single point which alone is necessary.
You know what this point is, I have repeated it too often,
It is that he must still leave himself after he has left everything else;
That he must make a sacrifice of all self-love <term>self-love: original: "amour propre" — in this context, it refers to the ego's tendency to center itself even in spiritual matters.</term>,

Let him finally banish himself from his own self,
And being raised thereby into a perfect state,

Following this Maxim, let him hold in very little esteem

Who, trampling everything underfoot, even defies his own self,
And breaking with himself to unite with his God,
Knows how, in all things and everywhere, to take the lowest place.

That to follow Jesus you must carry your Cross:
For many mortals these are harsh laws,

<meta>This page continues the poetic rendition of Book II, Chapter XII, "The Royal Way of the Holy Cross." <page-num>136</page-num>
<header>THE IMITATION OF</header>

These are troubling words for a soul that loves itself;
But it will be even harsher and more troubling,
For whoever has not followed this thorny path, <note>The "thorny path" refers to the life of suffering and self-denial modeled by Jesus, contrasting with the "broad road" of worldly pleasure.</note>
To hear on the last day these final words:
*Away from me, wretched ones, away, cursed criminals,*
*Who made idols of fleeting goods;*
*Tumble far from me into eternal fires.* <note>original: "Loin de moi... feux éternels" — A poetic paraphrase of Matthew 25:41: "Depart from me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels."</note>

On that astounding day, which from the depths of the dust
Shall make our bones come forth, reunited with their flesh,
Shepherds and Kings, equally troubled,
Shall fear the terrifying thunderbolt of this Decree.
The opened abysses of celestial severities
Will fill every heart with equal trembling
Where this august Cross is not imprinted;
But those who now follow its banner,
Will then see everything shudder with a most just fear,
And in this vast terror will have no part.

This sign high in the sky, all shining with light,
When God shall show Himself upon His Tribunal, <note>The "Tribunal" refers to the Judgment Seat of Christ, where all souls are said to be evaluated at the end of time.</note>
Shall be the blessed beacon for His Elect,
And the radiant banner for the victorious.
Then the worthy servants of the Crucified,
Who, to be His true imitators here below,
Made themselves voluntary slaves of the Cross,
Shall have full raptures at His sight,
And shall expect only eternal rewards,
When the rest shall fear eternal punishments.

The Cross opens the entry to the throne of glory,
By it, this Kingdom is easy to win;
Love then this Cross through which you are to reign,
In it is salvation, life, and victory:
The invincible support against all enemies,
The promised outpouring of celestial sweetness,
And the strength of the soul have their sources in it;

The spirit finds its joy and its tranquility there,
It sees there the height and the model of all virtues,
And the perfection of our holiness.

It is this alone that must be followed;
You would deceive yourself to take any other goal;
Outside of it, there is no salvation for your soul,
Outside of it, no hope for eternal life.
I wish to tell you, and tell you a hundred times:
If you do not wish to perish, take up your Cross upon you;
Follow the painful tracks of the Crucified,
And the gifts attached to this glorious burden <note>The "glorious burden" (glorieux faix) refers to the Cross, which is viewed as heavy with suffering yet lightened by the promise of divine reward.</note>
Stirring the treasures of His Grace within your heart,
Will lift you to Heaven, to live there forever.

He walked before you, He carried His own;
He showed you the example by dying there for you,
And this death leaves you a law of love
To carry one just like it, and to die upon your own. <note>The author encourages "dying to oneself," a common mystical theme meaning the abandonment of selfish desires to live for God.</note>
If you die with Him, you shall live with Him;
The part you take in His mortal sorrow,
You shall also have in the greatness following His victory:
The measure is equal, and it is in vain
That one imagines having a share of His glory in Heaven
When one has not shared in His torment here below.

Thus, to reach this full joy,
Everything consists in the Cross, and everything lies in dying;
It is through this that Heaven allows itself to be conquered,
And God has made no other way to save us.
True life and solid peace,
The inner calm of our sweetest desires,
True rest, finally—it is the Cross that gives it:
Learn then without ceasing to mortify yourself, <term>mortify: the practice of self-denial or "putting to death" worldly impulses to strengthen the spirit.</term>
And know that whoever aspires to the crown,
Must trust in the Cross alone.

Look back upon the image of all the ages,
Walk on every side, seek in every part,
Raise your gaze to the highest Heavens,
Plunge your thought to the depths of the Earth:
See the heights of contemplation,
See the certainty of humiliation,
Leave nothing unseen in all of Nature;
You will find no other choice to make,
You will find no surer route,
Nor any path higher than that of the Cross.

Go further still, and dispose of everything absolutely,
Rule everything by your order according to your desire;
You will not lack objects of displeasure,
You will find something to suffer everywhere.
Whether by force or by will, whatever one may hope,
The inevitable Cross presents itself to us everywhere,
Always something to suffer, and something to sigh for;
And we always feel some pain in the body,
Or some trouble in the soul even more stubborn,
Which seem, in turn, to deliver us to misfortune.

God will sometimes leave you without tenderness <note>In mystical theology, this "lack of tenderness" refers to "spiritual dryness," a period where the believer no longer feels the emotional comfort or joy of their faith, serving as a test of devotion.</note>,
Often you will be tested by your neighbor;
Often sunk within yourself by sorrow
You will yourself become a burden to your own weakness:
Often, without remedy and without relief,
You will encounter nothing in this overwhelm
That can cure or relax your pain:
Your only recourse then must be to endure
Through a patience equal to this distress,
As long as it pleases your God to make it last.

His loving orders thus wish to instruct you
To suffer bitterness, both full and without sweetness,
So that your virtue lets your whole heart go
Wherever His sacred will is pleased to lead it:

Its misery receives the means to be consoled!

### CHAPTER II.

*That Truth speaks within the heart without any noise of words.*

Speak, speak, Lord, your servant listens;
I say your servant, for indeed I am;
I am, I want to be, and walk in your path,
Both by day and by night.

Fill me with a spirit that makes me understand
What your holy wills command of me,
And reduce my desires to the single desire of hearing
Your high truths.

But disarm your divine eloquence of lightning,
Let it flow without noise into the heart of me;
Let it have the living abundance of dew,
And its lovely sweetness. <note>The poet contrasts the "noise" of worldly language with the "dew" of divine grace, which nourishes the soul silently.</note>

You feared it, Hebrews, you believed that lightning,
And death followed it, and would lay all to waste,
You who in the Wilderness could not resolve
To hear Him speak. <note>This refers to the biblical account in Exodus 20:18-19, where the Israelites were terrified by the thunder and lightning on Mount Sinai and asked Moses to speak to them instead of God.</note>

From a labor that leads you where such glory shines:

There are some minds whose inquisitive pride <note>original: "orgueil curieux." In 17th-century spirituality, "curiosity" was often considered a vice—the desire to know hidden divine mysteries or useless information rather than focusing on one's own moral failings.</note>

It makes the heaviest burdens feel light,

Gives a thousand sweetnesses to bitterness itself.

This love of Jesus is noble and generous,
It makes a man in love with great actions,

Always aspire more and more toward perfection.
It always goes upward to seek true charms,
It treats with contempt everything it sees as low,

Even to the point of suffering no <term>worldly affections</term>, <note>original: "affections mondaines." These are emotional or material attachments to the world that "cloud" the soul's vision.</note>

Take away the sight of Heaven from their secret gaze;
Lest a frivolous interest in temporal things
Abate the desires it pushes toward eternal ones;

<note>The vocabulary below highlights the key spiritual concepts explored in this poetic meditation.</note>

**Love of Jesus**: A divine, selfless affection that empowers the soul.
**Disciplines**: Spiritual exercises or corrections used to train the soul.
**Vices and passions**: The internal inclinations toward sin or worldly distraction.
**Perseverance**: The steady persistence in faith despite suffering.
**Treasure**: A metaphor for the incomparable value of divine love.
**Burdens**: The trials of life made light by love.
**Worldly affections**: Attachments to the physical world that hinder spiritual sight.
**Temporal things**: Things belonging to time and the earth, as opposed to the eternal.

### CHAPTER IX.

*That everything must be referred to God, as our final end.*

**I**f you wish to smooth the path to happiness,
Choose me as your sovereign and final end;
Purify your desires through this intention:
Your flames <note>In 17th-century spiritual poetry, "flames" often represent the heat of one's passions or the intensity of one's desires.</note> will become as straight and pure as those desires—
Those flames that your foolish passion often
Bends back toward yourself, or toward created things;
And which hold only weakness, aridity, <term>aridity: a spiritual state of "dryness" or lack of emotional consolation during prayer.</term> and listlessness,
As soon as you lower your heart to seek your own self.

It is to me, it is to me that you must refer
The most exquisite goods, the strongest graces;
To me, who gives everything and holds everything in my hand.
To use all things well, look upon each thing
As an outflow of this sovereign good,
Which I alone form, and which I alone dispense;
And take the streams that I pour upon you
As guides toward the source to which you owe their waters.

Whoever climbs that high does not find me stingy;
The small and the great, the poor along with the rich,
May draw from it equally and without ceasing;
My generous love opens it to all without reserve.
I love to give my goods, I love to show favor,
But I desire, in my turn, to be loved and served;

### CHAPTER XII.

->*How one must practice patience and combat the passions.*<-

From what I can see, Lord,
I have great need of patience,
Against the harsh experience,
To which this life binds a heart.

It is nothing but a gulf of evils,
Of troublesome and contrary accidents, <note>In 17th-century usage, "accidents" refers to unexpected events or external circumstances, often of a negative nature.</note>
An overwhelming weight of miseries,
From which labor follows labor.

I finish no battles there
That every moment does not renew,
And my peace drags along with it
The war attached to my footsteps.

Even the cares taken to strengthen it
Are in effect nothing but a war,
And my entire stay upon the Earth,
But an occasion to groan.

You speak truly, my child; nor do I wish
That you seek on Earth a peace without battles,
A rest without tumult, a calm without storm,
Where Fortune <term>Fortune</term> always shows the same face, <note>The author uses "Fortune" to describe the personified, fickle nature of worldly circumstances that human beings cannot control.</note>
And seems, by the course of its events,
To enslave itself to your satisfactions.

I want to see you in peace, but amidst hardships <term>traverses</term>, <note>From the French "traverses," referring to obstacles, setbacks, or "crosses" that one must cross or endure.</note>
Amidst the changes of various fortunes;
I want to see your calm there, and that adversity
Serves to strengthen you in tranquility.

<summary>The Disciple laments that life is a constant cycle of misery and conflict, to which Jesus responds that true peace is not the absence of struggle, but the maintenance of calm amidst adversity.</summary>

### CHAPTER XIV.

*On the Consideration of the secret judgments of God, for fear that we may fall into vanity because of our good actions.*

Lord, you cause your judgments to thunder over me,
All my shaken bones tremble under their threat;
My tongue is mute from it, & my heart, all of ice,
Has nothing left but shudders to explain itself.

My soul, terrified at the flash of their lightning,
Wanders in fear, & allows itself to be overwhelmed;
Everything it foresees only serves to trouble it,
And my confused spirit knows not what to resolve.

I remain motionless in this mortal dread,
And everywhere beneath my feet I find a precipice;
I see what my crime is, & what your justice is,
And I know that the Heavens are not pure before you. <note>original: "le Ciel n'est pas pur devant toi." This is a scriptural allusion to Job 15:15: "Behold, he putteth no trust in his saints; yea, the heavens are not clean in his sight."</note>

Your Angels before you were not without stain,
And you allowed nothing to your pity for them:
Being more criminal, would I be more fortunate,
I, whom no shadow hides from this justice?

Into the deepest hollow of the abyss it has tripped
Those Stars so brilliant with glory & light; <note>The "Stars" refer to the fallen angels, such as Lucifer, who were once the most radiant beings in creation before their pride led to their fall.</note>
And I, Lord, & I, who am but dust, <term>Dust: (original: *poussiere*) A common biblical reference to Genesis 3:19, reminding the reader of human frailty and mortality.</term>
Shall I believe with reason that I am dearer to you?

The great devout ones like them make strange falls,
I have seen their most noble works degenerate,

It serves as a warning against spiritual pride by emphasizing human insignificance and the history of those more "brilliant" who have fallen.</summary>

The very care to avoid it makes us run toward it:
But as soon as your hand deigns to help us,
We return to life, & win the crowns.

Our fire grows cold, you lend it flames;

O nothingness, O true void, yet of such extreme weight!

Which your great judgments open on every side;

If they saw their fragile flesh before you?
How could they allow a mass of clay <note>original: "masse d'argile." A biblical allusion to the creation of man from the dust of the ground (Genesis 2:7).</note>
To swell with pride against the hand that just formed it?

A heart truly yours is never led astray;
And whoever once tastes the spirit of truth,
Who can submit to it with sincerity,
Can no longer taste empty praise.

Yes, when your truth has fully submitted them to you,
The good said of them never lifts them up:
Though an entire world praises them, an entire world only succeeds
In strengthening the contempt they have conceived for themselves.

As soon as they fix all their hope in God,
Praises no longer have any power over them;
They hear their sweetness, but without being moved,
Without ever lending them the slightest indulgence.

Thus, all flatterers are nothing by themselves;
The incense they offer is as perishable as they are;

# CHAPTER XX.

*Of the acknowledgment of one's own infirmity, and the miseries of this life.*

To my shame, Lord, I confess to you
What is my unrighteousness, and what is my weakness;
I am willing to serve as a witness against myself:
A small thing casts me down, a small thing saddens me;
And in all my desires, if I am resisted even slightly,
A proud grief suddenly dictates its law to me. <note>original: "un orgueilleux chagrin" — "Chagrin" here implies a mixture of bitter annoyance and spiritual gloom caused by pride.</note>

It is in vain that I resolve to act with courage,
The smallest whirlwind makes me fear the storm,
And overthrows my firmest resolve with dread;
Out of anguish and spite, I abandon my path,
And delivering myself up to that which I fear,
I make myself the plaything of both winds and waves.

It is on all sides exposed to your sight;

She <note>Referring to the human soul or the "weakness" mentioned on the previous page.</note> does not consider at all what makes it <note>The World.</note> hateful:

The sweetness that God is pleased to pour down from on high
Are riches that her spiritual lethargy <note>original: "langueur" — a state of spiritual listlessness or lack of zeal.</note> has never tasted;
She has never seen what charm this great Master possesses,
Nor how much the virtue that fears to appear too much <note>A reference to the "hidden life" or humility, a core concept in 17th-century French spirituality.</note>

It is this which bestows upon them that exquisite sweetness,
And by His own voice, God Himself has promised it
To whoever can stand firm in this noble purpose.

By this, our fervor, finally better enlightened,
Casts a steady gaze upon the world,
Which its flattering glare could not dazzle;
We see how it deceives, and deceives itself,
We see it lose itself, and lose what it loves
Amidst the false goods it thinks it enjoys.

*That one must find rest in God above all goods and all gifts of Nature and Grace.*

My soul, it is in God above all things
That you must rest in everything, everywhere, and always;

There is no rest elsewhere that is not sinful,
And He alone is the eternal rest of the Saints.

Make it so then, lovely Author of all Nature,
That in You I find more rest than in any creature;
More than in the longest happiness of full health,

Above whatever pleasure might be promised
By the sweetest hope or the dearest desire;
Above all the gifts that Your liberal hand

Above the support it receives from the Archangels;

Above what remains imperceptible to the eyes;

Everything we possess here below, beyond the soul itself,
Is but an outpouring of your full abundance:
You alone gave us birth, and You alone sustain
Us, and Your blessings everywhere reveal Your generosity,
Which lavishes every kind of good upon us.

If inequality is found in their distribution,
If one receives more, and another receives less,
Everything is nonetheless a result of Your care,
And both this "more" and "less" owe You the same homage.
Without You, the smallest gift cannot be obtained,
And he who receives the most must better guard himself
Against that sweet pride <note>In 17th-century French spirituality, "sweet pride" (*doux orgueil*) refers to the subtle, almost pleasant vanity that arises from having plenty, which can quietly lead a soul away from God.</note> to which abundance invites us;
And no matter how much he is advantaged above others,
He must neither puff himself up with his own merit,
Nor treat the most poorly-endowed with contempt.

A man is all the better for attributing less to himself;
He is all the greater as he humbles himself more,
And as he blesses You for so many gifts received,
He recognizes within himself his own naked poverty <note>"Naked poverty" refers to the spiritual state of realizing that without God’s grace, the human soul possesses nothing of value.</note>.
It is through ardent zeal, it is through humility,
It is through the holy confession of his unworthiness
That he draws more powerful graces upon himself;
And he who can judge himself the weakest of all,
Strengthens himself all the more to walk in Your footsteps,
And goes all the higher the more he takes the lowest place.

He for whom Your hand seems more stingy <note>original: "avare." Corneille uses this provocative term to describe the perspective of someone who feels they have received few worldly or spiritual gifts.</note>,
Must see it without sadness and endure it without boredom;
And without feeling envy for those richer than he,
Wait with respect for what Your hand prepares for him.
Instead of murmuring against Your will,
It is for him to praise Your divine goodness,
Which gives all its presents without regard for persons <note>A reference to the biblical concept that God is no "respecter of persons" (Acts 10:34), meaning He does not show favoritism based on worldly status or wealth.</note>;

<summary>This page explores the spiritual ethics of inequality, arguing that whether one receives much or little from God, the proper response is humility and gratitude. It teaches that spiritual greatness is achieved not through possessing gifts, but through acknowledging one's own unworthiness and taking the "lowest place."</summary>

# JESUS CHRIST. BOOK III.

->P 4<-

You give freely and even anticipate our desires,
But it is also right that the portion one receives
Depends solely on Your good pleasure.

Just as from a source of inexhaustible wealth,
Everything flows to us from Your kindness <term>benignité: a 17th-century term for God's generous and fatherly benevolence</term>;
Without owing anything to anyone, Your kindness bestows upon everyone,
And no matter what she gives, she remains worthy of adoration.
You decide what is best to give to each person,
And whether You choose to expand or limit Your gifts,
Your divine order has reasons that govern all things;
Our minds are ill-suited to question Your choices,
And You alone know the reasons for "more" or "less,"
You who alone know the true worth and value of every soul.

Thus, I wish to consider it a supreme favor
To possess few of those gifts that shine outwardly—
Those gifts the World <note>In this spiritual context, "the World" refers to secular society and its materialistic values, which are often seen as distractions from God.</note> prizes as treasures,
Which are followed everywhere by human praise.
I know that quite often these are but false glimmers,
And that poverty itself is one of Your gifts,
Bearing the priceless mark of Your hand;
And that among mortals, being brought low <note>The original French "ravalé" implies being diminished in social status or humbled.</note>
Provides less a reason for sorrow and complaint
Than a worthy reason to live in spiritual consolation.

You did not choose Your friends or Your companions <term>commensaux: literally "table-fellows," those invited to eat at the same table; intimate associates</term>
From among those surrounded by gold or ivory;
But from the lowest ranks and the humblest labors,
Which the proud World has banished from its glory.
Your Apostles, Lord, are clear witnesses to this—
They, to whom You entrusted the care of Your flock,
And whom Your hand ordained as Princes of the Earth.
From what high social order did You pull them?
And what was the royal purple <note>In the ancient world, purple dye was extremely expensive and reserved for emperors and kings. The poet contrasts this with the humble life of the disciples.</note> of John and Peter,
But a worn-out boat and torn fishing nets?

**Vocabulary:** kindness (benignité), poverty (pauvreté), Apostles (Apôtres), John (Jean), Peter (Pierre), providence, grace.

### CHAPTER XXIV.

*That one must not have curiosity regarding the actions of others.*

Banish, my son, from your mind
This wandering and sterile curiosity; <note>In this context, "curiosity" refers to a meddlesome interest in the affairs, sins, or reputations of other people rather than focusing on one's own spiritual life.</note>
Its useless eagerness
Can stifle the care for what is prescribed to you:
If you have but one thing to do,
What do the successes of this or that person matter to you?
Prefer the necessary to the superfluous,
And follow me, without thinking of what another does.

Whether one be humble, or whether he be vain,
Whether he speaks, or acts in such or such a way,
Once again, what does it matter to you?
Have I placed his conduct, or his tongue in your hand?
Have you any part in his shame?

### CHAPTER XXV.
#### *In what true Peace and true progress consist.*

I said it once before, *I leave you my peace,
I give it to you all*, <note>original: "Je vous laisse ma paix, Je vous la donne à tous," referencing the Gospel of John 14:27.</note> and the gifts I give
Have nothing perishable, like those of the World;
All love this peace, all would wish to find it,
But not everyone seeks the secret upon which is founded
The benefit of acquiring and preserving it.

My peace is with the humble, with the kind heart;
If you wish to possess such a divine happiness,
Join much patience to these two virtues:
But this is not yet enough to obtain it;
Lend me then, my son, a moment of silence,
And I will teach you the whole art of reaching it.

Keep a severe bridle on all your appetites, <note>Refers to worldly cravings and bodily desires that distract from spiritual focus.</note>
Take exact care of everything you say,
Examine no less everything you wish to do;
And give to your desires as an immutable law,
That their unique object be the good of pleasing me,
And their unique goal to seek only me.

<summary>Jesus instructs the soul to prepare for his arrival through prayer and humility, then defines true peace as a state found only in the humble and patient heart that seeks solely to please God.</summary>

# JESUS CHRIST. Book: III.

->Do not trouble yourself with the actions of others,<-

But do not be mistaken: to live exempt from misfortune,
The heart free of sorrows, and the body from pain,
To never be troubled by any anxiety—
This is not a true calm in these earthly places:
And this gift belongs only to the beatitude <note>Supreme blessedness; the highest state of holiness and joy.</note>
That I reserve for you in Heaven for Eternity.

So when you see yourself without any displeasure,
When everything on all sides responds to your desires,
When nothing bitter or contrary happens to you,
Do not yet estimate that you have found peace,
Nor that everything in you is so good, so salutary,
That there is cause to place you among the number of the perfect. <note>In historical spiritual traditions, "the perfect" refers to those who have reached the highest stage of the spiritual life, characterized by constant union with God.</note>

Do not believe yourself, either, to be great or well-loved,
Simply for feeling a zeal so inflamed
That by force of tenderness it bathes you in tears;
The true affection for solid virtues
Does not consist in all these little charms, <note>Often referred to as "sensible consolations"—the emotional feelings of sweetness in prayer that may not reflect actual spiritual depth.</note>
Nor in your advancement, nor your perfection.

*In what then, you ask me, does it fully consist,*
*This perfection, and this advancement?*
*This true peace, where is it found?*
I truly wish to teach it to you: It is, in the first place,
To offer yourself entirely with a truly faithful heart
To the sovereign orders of the will of your God.

This submission to my sacred decrees
Must close your eyes to all your interests,

### CHAPTER XXIX.

->*How one must invoke God and bless Him when tribulation draws near.*<-

You will it, O my God, that this unrest <note>Original: "inquiétude." In a spiritual context, this refers to a lack of inner peace or a state of spiritual agitation.</note>,

It is enough that your arm deigns to be my support;

How many agitations tear at my heart!
It finds itself in the midst of a strange torture,

Gentle and kind Father, who knows my weakness,
What must I say in this overwhelming state?
You see on all sides how much hardship presses upon me;
Save me, my Savior, from such a cruel torment.

So that your glory may take on more brilliance,
When, after having seen my constancy cast down,
It will be seen, through you, defying <note>Original: "brayer." This is likely an archaic spelling or an error for "braver" (to defy or brave), as the context describes steadfastness overcoming the trial.</note> that which strikes it down.

# JESUS CHRIST. Book III.

Stretch out then this powerful and gracious <note>Original: "débonnaire." In the 17th century, this term described a person of high rank who was exceptionally kind, gentle, or merciful, rather than its modern English connotation of being lighthearted or sophisticated.</note> hand

Your almighty hand is still as strong

She <note>In French, "the hand" (la main) is feminine, and the poet personifies it here.</note> who, taming the cruelty of my ills,

Lest I be completely beaten down by them.

Yes, your pity, my God, sustaining my courage,
Can make it the victor over their harshest assault;
And the more this change is a painful labor for me,
The more I see it as easy for the hand of the Most High.

### CHAPTER XXX.
#### *How one must seek God’s help, with the confidence of recovering His grace.*

Come to me, my child, when you are not well;
Make me the secret confidant of your anguish;
In the darkest days, whatever blow it deals,
I am always that God who consoles and strengthens:
But the thing that holds back these consolations
Which I pour from on high upon afflictions,
Is that—even though they are the only remedies—
You are a bit slow to turn to me to ask for them.
Before I see you prostrate at my feet,
Calling out to me in the midst of the troubles that torment you,
You make vain attempts at all the distractions
The World promises for your deep sorrow,
And this straying of your unwise desires
Seeks on the outside for what I offer within.

Thus, what you do is of little use to you;
Thus, what you do exposes you to further ills,
Until your remaining faith remembers
That I know how to protect anyone who hopes in me;
And that there is no help elsewhere that does not yield to mine,
Nor any fruitful counsel, nor lasting remedy.

### CHAPTER XXXI.

*On the contempt of all Creatures, to rise to the Creator.*

Lord, if until now you have shown me a thousand Graces, <note>In 17th-century theology, "Graces" refers to divine assistance or spiritual gifts given to the soul.</note>
It is not time for you to grow weary of them,
I have need of a help even more powerful;
Since I must rise above Nature, <note>Here, "Nature" represents the physical world, human instincts, and ego that keep the soul tethered to Earth.</note>
And take a flight so high, that no creature
Has anything to hinder me.

Toward this happy effort I prepare myself in vain;
As long as down here the smallest thing
Can pull me down toward its weak attractions,
The imperceptible yoke of an unworthy constraint
Will not allow me that holy liberty,
Which makes us fly up to you.

Your David wanted no obstacle to this flight,
And asked this miracle of you,
When in his troubles he spoke these words:
*Who will give me wings like a Dove;*
*And from the midst of the evils, under which my heart sinks,*
*I shall fly away to my rest?* <note>original: "Qui pourra me donner des aîles de Colombe; Et du milieu des maux... Je volerai jusqu'au repos?" This is a poetic paraphrase of Psalm 55:6 (Psalm 54:7 in the Vulgate Bible).</note>

This bird is the visible portrait of true calm,
Nothing is seen so peaceful
As the simplicity painted in its eyes:
Nothing is seen as free as a true zeal,
Which, without desiring anything, rises on swift wings
Above all these lowly places.

One must therefore fully abandon oneself,
Tear oneself away from everything one loves,

### CHAPTER XXXII.

*That one must renounce oneself and all kinds of desires.*

->In its most perfect state.<-

But when I show it to you, must you lose heart?
Should you not rather move toward it with joy,
Or at least sigh after such happiness?

Ah, if I saw you reach this point,
Where <term>self-love</term> <note>original: *amour propre*. A recurring theme in 17th-century spirituality, referring to the ego or pride that centers the self rather than God.</note> was thoroughly uprooted within you;
Where you remained firm under my will,
And under that of the Father to whom I have given you!

Then you would please me, and the course of your life
Would be all the sweeter for your being submissive;
You would see it followed by a thousand true pleasures,
And flow in peace amidst a thousand enemies.

But you still have many things to give up;
For if you cannot resign everything to me entirely,
You will never acquire what you intend,
Never will you obtain the fulfillment of your desires.

<summary>In this passage, Christ explains that true spiritual peace is found by renouncing worldly desires and "self-love," a difficult path that requires a lifetime of discipline. ### CHAPTER XXXVI.
*Against the vain judgments of men.*

Fix in me all the attachments of your heart,
Without worrying yourself about those vain judgments
That men will want to make;
Innocence owes them an eternal contempt,
When the upright and sincere soul
In its secret recesses <note>original: *replis secrets*; literally "secret folds," referring to the deepest, most private parts of one's conscience.</note> has nothing criminal.

When one suffers unjust talk for my sake,
The hardest suffering has charming returns,
Which savor of beatitude: <term>beatitude: A state of perfect blessedness or the direct experience of God’s presence.</term>
The humble person who trusts in his God, more than in himself,
Never finds anything harsh therein,
And raises all the more his hope and his faith.
Many speak much without being well-informed;
And their temerity sows so many false rumors,
That one puts very little stock in so many words:

### CHAPTER XXXVII.

->*Of pure and entire self-resignation, to obtain liberty of heart.*<-

### JESUS-CHRIST. Book III.

In vain does an ancient abuse swell their power,
They know how to bend them back to that sincere duty
Which the sovereign Author saw fit to prescribe;
And since in creating all things He neglected nothing,
They know how to cast back under such a righteous rule
All that a long-standing disorder might have set loose.

Stand firm above all events;
Let not their outward appearance take you by surprise,
And never let your fleshly senses dictate your feelings
Regarding what you are shown or what you hear,
For fear of being blinded by their illusion;
Act as Moses did on every occasion:
Come and consult your God about all your conduct.
His answer will often deign to enlighten you,
And you will emerge with a soul better instructed
In all that is happening, and all that must be hoped for.

This great Lawgiver <term>Legislateur: A title for Moses, who delivered the Ten Commandments</term> who proclaimed my laws,

No matter the great perils that entangled him,
Or the seditions that hemmed him in,

Redouble the fervor of your zeal in your times of need.

Joshua his disciple, and the children of Israel,

They lost the blessings that had been promised to them,

I see as the only support for my highest efforts
The nothingness <note>original: *néant*</note> that I am, and the nothing from which I come;
And to found one's glory thus upon nothing itself,
Is a vanity that reaches the extreme.

O pernicious wind, O poison of the spirits!

Your deceptive attractions draw all our steps away

And the soul, unworthily stained by your breath,
Is stripped by you of the Graces <term>Graces: In 17th-century theology, these are the divine influences that sanctify the soul and enable virtuous living.</term> of its master.
Yes, our soul, Lord, though it is your portrait <note>Referring to the biblical concept that humans are made in the "image and likeness" of God.</note>,

And its greed for empty praises
Deprives it of the virtues that made it equal to the Angels.

One ought to rejoice, and find glory;
But it is in you alone that everything must be grounded:
In you alone, not in oneself, must one endlessly take
True glory and holy joy;
Attribute to you alone, and not to one's own virtue,
The most solid radiance with which one is clothed;
Praise the Author of Nature <term>Author of Nature: A traditional title for God as the creator of the physical and spiritual laws of the universe.</term> in all his gifts,
And see only him in every creature.

I desire it, O my God: if I do any good,
Let my name be suppressed so that yours may be praised;
Let the entire Universe, by common consensus,
Exalt your works upon the contempt of my own;
Let my name be unknown even in this very work <note>Corneille, the poet, reflects here on his own act of writing this book, expressing a desire for his authorship to be forgotten in favor of God's message.</note>,
So that yours alone may be better adored;
Let your Holy Spirit alone have all the glory,
Without any praise honoring my memory,
And let anyone who wishes take possession, in my eyes,
Of any honor that might otherwise return to me.

<summary>In this poetic meditation, the speaker denounces the "poison" of vanity and pride, arguing that all human virtue belongs to God. The poet specifically prays that his own name be forgotten so that only God's glory remains, even regarding the book he is currently writing.</summary>

Is that which your holy empire creates;
Which your hand alone grants to your true servants,
And which can suffer no human mixture.
These temporal honors which make the soul vain,
These proud exteriors of worldly grandeur,
Once compared to your eternal glory,
Are nothing but the amusements of strayed minds.

O supreme truth, and always adorable;
Immense mercy, and always ineffable;
I do not claim in my fragility
Any other mercy, or any other truth.
To you, Holy Trinity, hope of the true Faithful,
To you be full praise, to you immortal glory;
May the whole Universe, may all the future,
May all Eternity praise and bless you.
These are all my vows, this is all the advantage
That my feeble labors ask for their share;
Too happy if the radiance of my most worthy work
Leaves my name obscure, to reflect back upon you.

<vocab>Grace, Jews, Holy Trinity, Eternity, glory, truth, mercy</vocab>

### CHAPTER XLIV.
*That one must not trouble oneself with external things.*

My son, it is good to ignore
Many things that take place,
And not to consider
A thousand events that pile up:
Be as if dead upon the Earth, and by the holy use
Of this indifference <note>original: *indifférence* — in this spiritual context, it refers to "holy indifference," a state of being detached from worldly outcomes to remain focused on God's will.</note> fertile in merit,
Keep yourself crucified to the things of the World,
And the things of the World like so many Crosses for you. <note>A reference to Galatians 6:14: "The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world."</note>

Turn a deaf ear to these noises
That an indiscreet murmur carries,
And think through days and nights
Upon the rest that I provide for you.
It is much better to withdraw your eyes
From everything that shocks you, or that can displease you,
Than to be all on fire over a contrary opinion,
For the frivolous honor of reasoning the best.

Leave to each their own sentiment,
Let them speak and discourse in their own fashion,
Hold your heart in me strongly,
And flee this inconvenient debate;
