### CHAPTER XLV.
#### *That one must not believe all persons, and that it is easy to slip in words.*

Send to my aid Your sovereign goodness,
Lord, against the evils that have chosen me for their target,
Since in vain would I place in human friendships
The hope of my salvation.

O my God, how many unfaithful ones I have found here below,
Whom I imagined were occupied with all my cares!
And how many I have met with true zeal
Where I believed it the least!

In vain, therefore, would one wish to found some hope
Upon the uncertain effect of their doubtful faith;

### CHAPTER XLVIII.
*Of the day of Eternity, and of the anguishes of this life.*

O blessed Abode of the heavenly City,
Where the day of Eternity reveals itself!
A Day that no darkness ever obscures,
A Day that the Star of Truth <note>original: *Astre de Verité* — A poetic reference to God or Christ as the source of all ultimate reality and enlightenment.</note> always illuminates,
A Day where a purified joy shines without ceasing,
A Day where an assured peace reigns without ceasing,
A Day always immutable, and whose holy radiance
Never degenerates into a contrary state!
Why does it not already shine? And to let it shine,
Why do the times not cease to lose and to produce? <note>This refers to the "generation and corruption" of the material world—the cycle of birth and death that characterizes temporary existence as opposed to eternity.</note>
Why does everything here that must end with their fall
Not already make way for this great future?
It shines, it shines already, but its vivid light
Is seen in its entirety only by the guests of Heaven:
As long as we remain exiled on Earth,
Only veiled rays of it fall upon us,
Distance blurs or dissipates the image
Of what escapes through a cloud,
And all that our eyes are permitted to see of it
Are reflected features spread by a mirror. <note>This is a direct allusion to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face."</note>

These inhabitants of Heaven know its delights,
While in these low places we drag out our tortures,
And an overwhelming burden of bitterness and sorrows
Makes of our most beautiful days frightful nights.

These days that time gives and steals away itself,
Long for those who know them, and short for those who love them,
Have for both a web of misfortunes,
From which anguish and pain are born in emulation.

To the cruel furies of a relentless war,
Where I always find myself in enemy country, <note>original: *païs ennemi* — In 17th-century devotional literature, the physical world was often described as a "hostile country" or "foreign land" where the soul is an exile far from its true home in Heaven.</note>

Pour into my displeasures some relief:
You know it is for You that my whole heart sighs,
You see it is to You that my whole heart aspires.
The World is a burden to me, and does nothing but increase
This weight of my ills which it tries to sweeten:
From it, nor from myself, should I expect anything;
I wish to possess You, yet I cannot comprehend You;
I barely take flight to attach myself to the Heavens,
Before a worldly care pulls me back down to these places,
And the poorly tamed forces of my passions <note>original: *passions* — Here meaning the unruly emotions and physical desires that distract the mind from God.</note>
Return me to the "sweetnesses" they had lent me:
The spirit takes the upper hand, but the weight of the flesh <note>original: *le poids de la chair* — A central concept in Christian asceticism where the physical body is viewed as a heavy weight that prevents the "light" soul from ascending to spiritual heights.</note>
Forces me to stumble down to the very bottom of everything.
Thus I struggle with myself, and I am a burden to myself,
Thus the disorder within me is extreme;
The flesh pulls downward, while the spirit pulls upward,
And the weaker part is the one that prevails.

How I suffer, Lord, when my soul—raised up
To the feet of its God who made and saved it—
Finds a damnable squadron of shameful feelings <note>original: *dannable escadron de sentimens honteux* — The author uses military imagery ("squadron") to describe the intrusive, distracting, or sinful thoughts that interrupt the focus of a person trying to pray.</note>

Just as the eye of faith turns toward what brings it joy;
What Nature <note>original: *Nature* — Here referring to "fallen" human nature or natural inclinations, which in this context are often seen as obstacles to divine grace.</note> loves, or what pleases through habit,
Is what most quickly presents its image to us;
And it rarely presents it without our touched spirit
Attaching itself effortlessly to where the heart leans.

Also, your own mouth has been pleased to tell me,

In its prosperity I find my joy,
And its setbacks stir my sadness.

If the pleasures of the senses seize my love,
What can flatter them occupies me night and day;
If I love the perfect knowledge of the spirit,
I make my conversation of everything that advances it;
In short, everything I love, and everything that pleases me,
Holds me as if enchained by a sweet interest:
I speak of it with pleasure, with pleasure I listen
To everything that can teach me to walk in its path,
And I carry the image home with pleasure,
Of everything that tickles and pricks my desire.

Banishes every creature <note>original: *toute la créature* — In 17th-century theological language, "the creature" or "creaturely things" refers to anything created (people, objects, worldly status) as opposed to the Creator.</note> to love you alone;

Anything that he himself loves to ask for,
Distrusts the flesh and the senses so much,
That by force of fervor the spirit crucifies them.

Raising his desires upon a contempt for the World,
He offers you a prayer <term>oraison: a form of mental or contemplative prayer where the heart speaks to God without necessarily using set formulas</term>, he offers you praises,
Worthy of mingling with those of your Angels,
Since in him your love, by its divine transports,
Smothers the earthly both within and without.

# CHAPTER XLIX.

### *Of the desire for Eternal Life, and how many blessings are promised to those who struggle.*

When you feel, my son, kindling in your heart
A loving desire for eternal bliss; <note>original: *beatitude* — A state of supreme happiness or blessedness, specifically the joy of seeing God in heaven.</note>
When your heart sighs for me with a sweet longing,
To see me without shadow, and without change:
When you feel it driven by impatient transports,
To see yourself freed from the prison of the body; <note>original: *la prison du corps* — A common theological metaphor in the 17th century, viewing the physical body as a temporary confinement for the immortal soul.</note>
And contemplate up close my infinite brightness;
Open your whole soul to this ambition,
And bring the united forces of your heart
To what this inspiration requires of you.

Above all, when you receive this loving desire,
Remember to return to me a million thanks, <note>original: *Graces* — Here used in the sense of "action de grâce" or thanksgiving for divine favor.</note>
To me, whose goodness deigns thus to choose you,
Deigns thus to draw you from among the lowly souls.
It is I, whose mercy bows my greatness
Even to visiting you, and creating this ardor,
Which has flowed into your breast from on high;
It is I who raise you up and sustain you,
Lest by your own weight your soul be dragged down
And embrace, instead of me, the earth from which you come.

Neither your efforts of spirit, nor those of your fervor,
Give birth to this desire that it pleases me to produce;
It is a pure effect of my high favor,
Of my divine countenance which deigns to shine upon you.
Use it to advance yourself with ease
Upon the path of virtues, and of humility;

<term>Eternal Life</term>: The state of everlasting existence with God.
<term>Beatitude</term>: The ultimate state of spiritual joy.
<term>Inspiration</term>: A divine influence directly moved into the mind or soul.
<term>Graces</term>: Acts of thanksgiving or the unmerited favor of God.
<term>Clemency</term>: Mercy or leniency.
<term>Virtues</term>: Moral excellence or righteousness.
<term>Humility</term>: The quality of having a low view of one's own importance; humbleness.

<summary>In this opening to Chapter 49, God explains to the disciple that the longing for heaven and the "prison-break" from the body is a gift of divine grace rather than a human merit. The soul is encouraged to use this inspired ardor to pursue virtue and humility rather than worldly things.</summary>

Are not all conceived purely to please me,
Nor do they all have my honor as their sole goal.

Your own even, your own, whose persistence
So often solicits me with such warmth,
And hastens the effects of my kindness
By the sincere admission of your little merit; <note>original: *peu de merite* — A central theme in 17th-century French spirituality, emphasizing that humans cannot "earn" God's favor through their own works alone.</note>
Your vows, I say, often, without realizing it,
Covering your self-interest with this humble duty,
Seek your own joy as well as my glory;
And this small amount of self-love that joins them
Immediately leaves upon them a stain dark enough
To keep them very far from perfection.

Ask therefore, my son, ask strongly
Not for what is convenient for you, and should satisfy you;
But for a success for me, and an outcome
Which is glorious to me, and worthy of pleasing me.
If you let your vows be ruled by a truly healthy spirit,
You will know how to submit them to all that I will,
Without considering anything that you desire,
And to prefer my order so well to your desire,
That you no longer speak, nor think, nor breathe,

**Book III.**

You must, despite yourself, accept his law,
Obey his order and follow his rule; <note>original: *empire* — rule or dominion.</note>
And that is what causes your most cruel torments,
When you feel your reason powerfully contradict,
And when you must accept such commands.

But do not think so much on the excess of these evils,
That you cannot see how a single moment ends them,
That their fruit finally surpasses the greatness of the labor,
And that the reward for them is entirely divine.
Instead of being a burden, instead of overwhelming you,
They will know how to create, they will know how to redouble
The sweetness necessary to soothe your pain;
And this moment of effort over your will
Will make it sovereign in Heaven forever
Over the infinite treasure of all my goodness.

In these shining Palaces that I alone fill
You will easily find in me alone all things;
You will see your wishes fulfilled just as quickly,
You will hold in your hand whatever you propose:
All kinds of goods in great profusion
Will be born there from a happy and clear vision, <note>original: *claire vision* — a reference to the "Beatific Vision," the direct perception of God which is the ultimate goal in Christian theology.</note>
Without fear that time will change or take them away;
Your will and mine will be but one will there,
And you will want nothing there that is fulfilled outside of me,
Nor for which your own interest dares to prevail alone.

There, no one will come to resist your desires,
No one will form a complaint against you;
You will find no obstacle there to overcome,
You will meet no subject of fear.
The desired objects, all offering themselves at once,
Will not cause your love or your choice to waver
Upon the tremors of your uncertain soul;
You will possess everything without needing to choose,
And you will lose yourself in full abundance,

Without fulfillment dulling the desire. <note>original: *émouffe le defir* — the poet refers to a classic theological paradox: in Heaven, the soul is completely satisfied ("full") yet never bored, possessing a "desire" that is constantly being met.</note>

### CHAPTER L.
*How an afflicted man must surrender himself into the hands of God.* <note>The word used in the original French is *desolé*, which in a 17th-century spiritual context implies a state of "desolation"—a profound sense of being abandoned by God or overwhelmed by internal and external trials.</note>

May your holy name be blessed, now and forevermore,
Let things happen exactly as you have decreed;
You have done this, O my God, because you willed it;
And everything you do is good.

It is not in others, nor is it in himself
That your servant should take any pleasure;
But in all the outcomes that you choose for him,
And in your supreme will.

You alone fill a heart with true contentment,
You alone are the rightful prize for my labors;
And the honor I seek, and the hope that gives me life
Have their foundation in you alone.

What do I see in myself, Lord, what can I see appearing there,
Other than what you bestow without my having deserved it?
And of that which your generosity gives and performs,
Are you not always the master?

I am poor, fragile, besieged by misfortunes,
From my earliest years, anguish has surrounded me,
And my soul sometimes abandons itself to sorrows,
Even to the unworthiness of tears. <note>original: *l'indignité des pleurs* — The poet suggests that while weeping is natural, a "servant of God" should ideally strive for a stoic or faithful composure that transcends such displays of grief.</note>

Often even, often in the midst of my tears,
What I suffer yields to what I foresee,
And the pitiless dread of a dismal future
Tears at me with the force of its alarms.

<note>This text is a poetic paraphrase of *The Imitation of Christ* by Thomas à Kempis, likely the popular French verse translation by Pierre Corneille. The style uses Alexandrine verse (12-syllable lines) to elevate the devotional experience into high art.</note>

### CHAPTER LII.

->*That man should not consider himself worthy of consola-*<-
->*tion, but rather of punishment.*<-

Lord, if I dwell upon the little I deserve,
I cannot hope for your consolations,
Nor that from the height of Heaven your secret visit
Might deign to soften the bitterness of my afflictions.

I was never worthy of it; and when you leave me
Bereft, poor, infirm, powerless, and bewildered;
You only do justice to my cowardly weaknesses,
And this sad abandonment gives me back what I am owed.

Even if an ocean of tears from my whole face
Could flow incessantly in great torrents,
I would have no right to the least of those charms
Which your goodness pours out when you come to console.

After having blackened myself with a million offenses,
Having made myself a rebel against your commandments,
You can owe me, as just rewards,
Nothing but harsh lashes of the whip, and long punishments. <note>The author uses "lashes of the whip" (coups de fouet) as a metaphor for divine discipline or the "scourging" of the soul to purify it of pride.</note>

Against the future wrath and the terrifying day; <note>A reference to the Day of Judgment.</note>
God comes to meet it, and fulfills its expectation,
With a kiss of peace that reunites their love.

### CHAPTER LIII.

->*That God’s grace is incompatible with a taste for earthly things.*<-

My grace is precious; and the impure alloy
Of outward attractions and worldly pleasures—
Those sweetnesses with which the Earth poisons one's courage—
Are the eternal object of its just disdain:
Grace does not suffer their harmful mixing,
And from the moment one thinks to unite them with it,
Grace immediately withdraws,
And yields the heart to those who wish to keep them.

Rid yourself then, my son, of all that is corruptible,
Banish far from you all such hindrances,
If you wish your heart to remain receptive
To the sweetest part of its full outpouring.
Plunged in retreat, and alone with yourself,

## CHAPTER LIV.

### *Of the various movements of Nature and Grace.*

Consider, my son, in all that happens,
->Between Nature and Grace,<-
The subtle movements opposed to one another;
Their images often cast in the same place,
->One confounded with the other,<-
Have features so similar and so little divided,
That the greatest Devouts <note>A "Devout" (*dévot*) refers to a person deeply committed to religious practice and spiritual discipline.</note>, after having exhausted themselves
->In assiduous research,<-
Can barely, whatever care they might give to it,
Have eyes sharp enough to discern them well.

### CHAPTER LVI.

*That we must renounce ourselves, and imitate Jesus Christ by bearing our Cross.*

As much as you are able to step away from yourself,
So much will you pass into my supreme being.
Just as the soul roots peace within itself,
When for all things without it extinguishes its desires;
So when within itself it leaves its own self behind,
It unites with me through such high merit.
I wish, therefore, to teach you how to properly detach yourself,
Without clothing yourself again, without seeking yourself anymore;
To instruct you to submit to my pure will,
Without contradiction, without clamor, and without murmur.

Follow me; I am the Life, the Way, and the Truth; <note>original: "Vie, & Voie, & Verité." This is a poetic rendering of the Latin *Ego sum via et veritas et vita* from the Gospel of John 14:6.</note>
One does not go without a way to the intended destination,
One does not live without life; one can know nothing
If the light of truth does not appear.

It is I who am the life for which you must aspire,
The supreme truth in which you must find assurance,
The way to follow in all things; but a way inviolable,
Truth beyond doubt, and life unending.

I am the straight way, whose righteous course
To reach Heaven suffers no detours;
I am the sovereign and sacred truth,
I am, finally, the life: true, happy, and uncreated. <note>The term "uncreated" (incréée) is a theological technicality referring to God's eternal nature, which exists without having been made by another.</note>
If you take my way well, and walk without straying,
The Truth will know how to fully set you free; <note>A reference to John 8:32: "And the truth shall make you free."</note>
You will see it in full, and its faithful clarity
Will serve as your guide to eternal life.

To know it well, listen, and believe my voice;

That which you see clearly enough I wish to be observed.
He who, well-instructed by these teachings,
Keeps a profound respect for my commandments,

## CHAPTER LVIII.

*That one must not seek to penetrate high mysteries, nor examine the secret judgments of God.*

Do not abuse, my son, your feeble lights <note>original: "lumieres" — a common metaphor for human reason or intellectual understanding.</note>,
By seeking to pierce the highest matters,
By seeking to enter into the deep secrets
Of the unequal appearance of my just decrees.
Do not seek to see what pressing reason
Makes my Grace act, or seem powerless;
Is stingy, or lavish; abandons, or sustains;
Never examine from where this distribution comes,
Nor why one thus languishes in misery,
And the other is so high above the common people.
There is no reasoning, there is no human effort,
That can penetrate my sovereign order;
Nor clarify the truth through long dispute
As to why I cherish, or why I persecute.

For one Saint or another, men feel more passion and esteem;

My hand has led them through temptations,
I alone have filled them with consolations,
I alone have given them perseverance,

All the glory must therefore be returned to me.
Thus, above all else, one must bless in them—
And above all else, praise—my infinite love,
Which, to show the abundance of its magnificence,
Raises them to such heights of glory and power;
And without any merit having first existed in them,
I predestine them to the rank I have reserved for them.

I must indeed weep and sigh after you,
And until the moment I expire,
Send all my prayers after you.

What other full confidence
Could promise me a help,
Which, for all the needs of human misery,
By a sovereign virtue,
Could dry up or limit the flow?

You alone are therefore my hope,
The support of my weakness,

And loves me with faithfulness.

Each seeks their own advantages,
You look only to mine;
And it is for my salvation that you pledge to love me,
That you calm all my storms,

Those are your words, sovereign Truth;

To let them pass into the depths of my heart;

Their holy impression touches me perceptibly:

### J E S U S-C H R I S T. Book IV.
Aa 3

If zeal acted then so strongly,

Excited the memory of your holy praise:

That this great Sacrament, that your precious Body
-> Must imprint deep within my soul! <-
And what must all Christian peoples not
Bring of respect, tenderness, and fire,

The Relics of the Saints, and their magnificent Temples
Make mortals run to a thousand and a thousand places;
They allow their ears and eyes to be charmed there,
By the lofty structure, and by their high examples;
They kiss on their knees the precious remains
Of their venerable flesh, and of their sacred bones,
-> Wrapped in gold and silk; <-
And I see you, my God, whole and entire upon the Altar,
You, the great Saint of Saints, you, the author of their joy,
You, the immortal Monarch of all the Universe!

Often even the spirit of these pilgrimages
Is nothing but a tickling of curiosity,
And the attraction that novelty always holds in itself,
Toward what has not been seen, thus draws hearts:
When such a vain motive pushes and leads them,
The longest labor yields little fruit,
-> And leaves nothing that amends; <-
Especially in those spirits foolishly eager,
Whom a too-light fervor obliges to these journeys,
Without any holy reflection upon their past crimes.

But in this Sacrament, your august presence,
True God-Man <note>original: "Homme Dieu." A theological term for Jesus, being simultaneously fully human and fully divine.</note>, makes the fruit certain,

# J E S U S-C H R I S T. Book IV.

Every time a worthily prepared heart
Brings to it full fervor and full reverence.
It does not go there either out of levity,
Nor through the "itch" of curiosity,
-> Nor by any other worldly lure: <-
All that leads it there is a firm faith,
It is the unshakable strength of a solid hope,
It is a burning love that has no object but you.

Invisible Creator of Earth and Heaven,
How great is the goodness you show toward us!
How favorable and sweet is your decree to the Chosen <note>The "Chosen" or "Elect" (French: *Elus*) refers to those whom God has called to salvation.</note>,
To offer them your incorruptible body <note>A reference to the Eucharist, which the author describes as "incorruptible" to contrast it with the physical remains or "flesh and bones" of saints mentioned on the previous page.</note> as food!
The charming miracles of your way of acting
Exhaust the strength of our understanding,
-> And do not allow themselves to be grasped: <-
This is what draws all the hearts of the Devout,
This is what pours such a tender love into their hearts,
This is what raises them to the highest fervors.

Thus these true Devotees, whose holy exercises
Apply all the activity of their care
To correcting in themselves that ease
Which Nature lends to the attacks of vice;
These rare servants, who have no other goal
Than to advance their lives on the path of salvation,
-> And to make their souls perfect; <-
Usually receive in this great Sacrament
A zeal more submissive to what you desire,
And the love of virtues more strongly imprinted.

Oh Grace, as wonderful as it is hidden,
Which the Faithful experience, and which cannot be tasted
By the lack of faith that stops to doubt,
Nor by the soul attached as a slave to vain pleasures!

# JESUS CHRIST. Book IV.
Aa 4

By your secret workings <note>original: "raisons secrets"; here referring to the hidden movements of grace or divine inspirations that guide the intellect.</note> the mind is better enlightened,
Far from the dark paths that had led it astray,
-> It resumes its rightful path; <-
Its beauty is restored, as well as its virtue;
And everything in it that the stain of sin <note>original: "crime"; in 17th-century devotional French, this often refers to the moral corruption of sin rather than a legal crime.</note> had spoiled
Returns to its original features the radiance they once had.

You descend sometimes with such abundance,
That once the soul is filled, a sweet overflowing
Spreads the reflection upon the body,
And animates it in turn by its lively influence:
The generosity <note>original: "prodigalité"; here meaning the unstinting or lavish nature of God’s giving.</note> of the divine hand
Wills that the whole man <note>A reference to the belief that the Sacrament benefits both the spiritual soul and the physical body.</note> have a share in this sovereign good,
-> In the midst of his weariness: <-
And from the worn-out body, the dragging languor,
In the overflow of this fullness
Often finds a treasure of new vigor.

As our cowardice <note>original: "lâchetez"; suggesting spiritual laziness or a lack of courage in pursuing the divine.</note>, as our lukewarmness,

And as his love can refuse nothing,
His goodness, always full and always magnificent,
Is a vast Ocean that can never be exhausted.

Bring to it, for your part, the strict attention
Of a renewed heart, to better prepare yourself;
And weigh maturely the greatness of a mystery,
On which depends your salvation, which you are about to work out.

### CHAPTER III.

See the eagerness of his humble duty,
And do not reject this ardor of his zeal,

### CHAPTER VII.

*Of the Examination of One’s Conscience, and the Purpose of Amending Oneself.*

Priest, whoever you may be, who goes to my Altar
To offer a living God to His immortal Father,
And to hold in your hands, and receive yourself,
The supreme mystery of my love for you;
Approach, but above all prepare within your breast
A strong humility, a sovereign respect,
A full and firm faith, a pure intention
To honor, to bless the Author of Nature: <note>A traditional title for God as the Creator of the universe.</note>
Cast an eye upon your inner self with care,
As an incorruptible Judge, as a faithful witness; <note>The text encourages a self-examination so rigorous that one treats oneself with the impartiality of a legal judge.</note>
And if a true concern for my honor touches you,
Ensure that a contrite heart, and the humble confession of mouth,
Know how to purge so well every hidden disorder,
That nothing may be reproached to you by remorse,

To raise your desires, without lowering them again,

And of all his sins I will lose the memory,
All will be so fully forgiven him by me
That he will have a place in the rank of my dearest friends.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### *On the offering of Jesus Christ upon the Cross, and on one’s own self-surrender.*

See how, completely stripped upon the Cross,
A pure and willing victim,
With both arms outstretched upon that infamous wood <note>original: "infame bois." This refers to the Cross, which in Roman times was a tool of execution reserved for the lowest criminals, hence "infamous."</note>
Long ago for your sins I offered myself to my Father;
Did I hold back anything of my very being,
If not so that my love might sacrifice it for you
To save you and to satisfy Him?

In the same way, you must with all your strength
Offer me each day in the Mass,
Every affection you can conceive,
With all its power and all its tenderness;
In this way you must, my son, sacrifice <term>sacrifice: originally "immoler," meaning to offer as a victim in a religious rite</term> in your turn
A heart that concerns itself with me alone,
And return me love for love.

Thus you will know how to win me over,
And what I ask of you most of all
Is that you take care to surrender yourself completely <term>surrender: "se resigner" here means "resignation" in the sense of total abandonment of one's will to God's will</term>,
To make of yourself a sincere offering;
No other gifts are sufficient for me,
I do not look to see if their value is great;
I seek you, and not your gifts.

Just as it would not be enough for you
To have a thousand advantages without me,
So you must not hope that I will value
Anything your tributes offer me without yourself;
Offer yourself entirely, and of your will,
In giving yourself to me, make no divisions,

## CHAPTER IX.

*That we must offer ourselves to God, with everything that is in us, and pray for the whole world.*

Heaven and Earth, and everything they contain;
Their effects and their virtues belong to you forever;
Everything is yours, Lord, everything moves under your law,

Is clothed before all time:

> Are you not alone all my peace,

The time and the manner of advancing a work,

Without there remaining even a little of myself within me
->In your holy presence!<-

Are you not that brazier, that divine flame,
->Which is never extinguished;<-
And whose living ray purifies, illuminates,
->Both the soul and its desires?<-

## CHAPTER XVII.

### *Of the ardent desire to receive Jesus Christ.*

With all the transports of which a
->soul<- is capable,
With all the ardor of a celestial flame,
With all the impulses of an affectionate zeal,
And the humble duties of a respectful heart,
I wish to approach your divine table,
I wish to bring there that true love,
That sincere fervor, and those firm resolutions,
Which so many illustrious Devout ones <note>The "Devout" (Dévots) refers to the faithful who are particularly dedicated to a life of prayer and piety.</note> once brought there,

<summary>The text concludes a prayer for divine love to consume the self and begins a new chapter on the intense, passionate desire a believer must feel when approaching the Eucharist.</summary>

So many Chosen ones, so many Saints, whose exemplary life
Knew best how to practice the great art of pleasing you.

->Yes, my God, my only good, my eternal<-
->love,<-
Paltry as I am, coward and criminal as I am,
I wish to receive you with as much zeal
As the most faithful of your Saints ever had;
And I would wish it were in my power
To have even more than they could conceive.

I know that my heart excites itself to these desires in vain,
They far exceed its strength and its merit;
But you see its reach, it goes to the very end,
It offers you what it has as if it had everything,
As if it alone held in its full power
These great efforts of love and gratitude,
As if it alone had all the pious desires
Which inflame the sighs of a purified soul,
As if it alone had all the secret ardor,
All the profound respect of a perfect virtue.

If what it offers you is little, at least it is its whole
->wealth,<-
It is giving you much to reserve nothing;
He who makes a full homage to you of all he has
Would offer you much more, if he were able:
I offer myself then entirely, and all that I can,
Without keeping anything for myself of all that I am;
I immolate myself, and for all my life,
At the foot of your Altars as a voluntary sacrifice. <note>original: "hostie" — In the 17th century, this term referred both to the consecrated bread of the Eucharist and to a sacrificial victim, echoing the "living sacrifice" mentioned in the Bible (Romans 12:1).</note>

Why can I not, O my God, supply my deficiency
By all that is highest in Heaven after you!
And to better express all that I desire,
But, O my Redeemer, will I dare to say it to you?
If I make to you the confession of my temerity, <note>In this context, "temerity" means a holy boldness or audacity in speaking to God.</note>

<summary>The speaker expresses a profound desire to receive the Eucharist with the same fervor as the Saints, offering their entire being as a "voluntary sacrifice" despite their personal unworthiness. The poem emphasizes that God accepts the sincerity of a heart that gives everything it has, even if that offering seems small.</summary>

Will you forgive it for having desired so much?
I desire today to receive this mystery, <note>The "mystery" refers to the Sacrament of the Eucharist.</note>
Just as your glorious Mother received you,
When, at the news an Angel came expressly to give her
Of the choice God made of her to be incarnated,
She answered him, both humbled and steadfast:
*I am but the Lord’s unworthy servant,* <note>original: "Je ne suis du Seigneur que l'indigne servante" — A poetic rendering of Mary’s response at the Annunciation: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word" (Luke 1:38).</note>
*Let him exert his absolute power upon me,*
*As you tell me, and as he has resolved.*
All the reverence she then had for you,
All the praise, love, and gratitude,
As much faith, hope, and purity as she possessed
During that worthy effort of her humility,
I would wish to bring all of it to this holy Table, <note>The "holy Table" (sainte Table) is a traditional term for the Altar or the act of receiving Holy Communion.</note>
Where you nourish your own with your adorable Body.

Why can I not at least, through a celestial fire,
Resemble your great Precursor even a little, <note>The "Precursor" is Saint John the Baptist, who "prepared the way" for Jesus.</note>
That illustrious Saint, whose high excellence
Seems to tip the scales above all others!
Why do I not have the impulses that animated him
When, still enclosed within the maternal womb,
Already impatient to prepare your way,
He felt your presence, and leaped for joy, <note>Referring to the "Visitation" (Luke 1:41), where the unborn John the Baptist leaped in Elizabeth’s womb when the pregnant Mary approached.</note>
But with a holy joy, and a leaping
Of which the Holy Spirit alone formed the movement.

When he later saw you to be as we are,
Conversing, teaching, living among men,
All inflamed with ardor, *Whoever loves the Bridegroom,* <note>original: "Quiconque aime l'Epoux" — A reference to John 3:29, where John the Baptist describes himself as the "friend of the bridegroom" who rejoices to hear the bridegroom’s voice.</note>
He cried out, *finds the sound of his voice so sweet,*
*That the loving tenderness of his charming tones,*
*As soon as he hears them, fills him with gladness.*

Why do I not have, like him, these high raptures,
These burning desires, and these great sentiments;
So that my whole heart, in a sublime transport

<header>J E S U S - C H R I S T. Book IV.</header>

Grant, Lord, that all those whom a true zeal
Animates to celebrate your worshipful mystery, <note>In this 17th-century context, "adorable" or "worshipful" refers to something that is the proper object of divine adoration.</note>
That all those whose love receives you with faith,
May obtain Grace for themselves, and call upon you for me.
When that holy union, for which their souls aspire,
Has filled them all with the sweetness they desire,
When they feel within themselves those consolations
That your blessings pour forth in great floods,
When they depart, enraptured, from your celestial table; <note>The "celestial table" refers to the Altar or the celebration of the Eucharist.</note>
Grant that they may take care to help a miserable soul,
And that their holy transports, before they come to an end,
May deign to remember a sinner such as I.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

*That man must not delve into the mystery of the Holy Sacrament with curiosity, but humbly imitate Jesus Christ, and submit his senses to Faith.* <note>In theological writings of this period, "curiosity" was often considered a vice—the intellectual pride of trying to use human reason to unravel divine mysteries that should be accepted by faith.</note>

You, who follow the dangerous paths of your senses,
And wish to penetrate everything through your own reasoning;
Know that to probe too deeply into so great a Sacrament,
Is to plunge yourself into an abyss of doubts.
Whoever dares to plumb the Majesty of a God,
In this vast Ocean of His immensity,
Will easily be shipwrecked, overwhelmed by His glory;
And you would seek in vain to understand His power,
Since a single word from His mouth accomplishes more
Than the whole of the human mind could ever conceive.

I do not forbid you the pious pursuit
Of the holy truths in which you must be instructed;
Their full knowledge is always of great benefit;

<page-num>438</page-num>
<header>THE IMITATION OF</header>

Provided that it is humble, and not curious; <note>In this 17th-century context, "curious" refers to "curiosity," which was seen as the vice of intellectual pride—trying to use human logic to explain divine mysteries.</note>
Provided that the faithful advice of the Church Fathers <note>The "Fathers" refers to the early influential theologians and bishops of the Christian Church.</note>
Is received and followed with submission,
You will make yourself happy, if you make yourself docile;
But happier still is that simplicity
Which avoids the difficult path of questioning,
And walks firmly under the laws of God.

How many has the world seen whose indiscreet audacity,
By dint of searching, has fallen into error,
And for having carried their insights too high,
Has pushed away the Grace of devotion!
Your God knows your weakness, and requires of you
Only the sincerity of a solid faith,
And a life obstinately set against the hatred of sin; <note>The original French "crime" refers here to moral sin or wickedness.</note>
And not those insights produced by high learning,
Nor that intelligence, both profound and sublime,
Which pierces through all the darkness of the obscure mystery.

If that which you can see beneath yourself
Is poorly understood by your confused mind,
How will you understand what has been placed above,
That which the supreme Monarch has reserved for Himself?
Restrain the tumultuous flight of this spirit;
To these rebellions of the presumptuous senses
Impose the amiable tyranny of faith; <note>The "amiable tyranny" of faith suggests a gentle but absolute rule of belief over the physical senses.</note>
Submit yourself entirely, leave to me all the care
Of pouring out my infinite knowledge upon you,
And I will measure the gift according to your need.

Often regarding the faith of such a deep mystery,
Many are strongly tempted to doubt;
But these temptations must only be attributed
To the suggestion of the common Adversary: <note>The "common Adversary" is a traditional title for Satan or the Devil.</note>
Do not trouble yourself with it; avoid the embarrassment
Where these perilous debates would throw your heart;

<page-num>439</page-num>
<header>JESUS CHRIST. Book IV.</header>

Whatever he <note>The "he" refers to the Tempter or the Devil, who uses intellectual doubt to shake the believer's faith.</note> dares to object to you, disdain to answer;
Believe me, believe my word, and that of my Saints;
This single secret is enough to confound him,
And will cause his designs to fail as he flees.

If he returns to the attack, and makes it more pressing,
Sustain all its effort without being troubled,
And remember that ultimately this redoubled assault
Is the sign of a soul advanced in virtue.
These hardened wicked men, these wretched sinners—
As he already holds them all securely for himself,
He never bothers to disturb them;
It is to the good that he attaches himself, and it is against their faith
That he deploys at every hour both his strength and his cunning,
To take from me, if he can, what he sees as entirely mine.

Come, and do not bring a wavering faith
That reason advises, and which holds everything suspect;
I want it simple and firm, with the humble respect
That your holy dread <note>In this context, "holy dread" (*sainte épouvante*) refers to a profound, religious awe and reverence before the mystery of the Eucharist.</note> owes to this great Sacrament.
Come then, and as a guarantee in this divine meal,
Of all that you believe and do not understand,
Take only my will, and my omnipotence;
I never deceive, and I cannot deceive,
But whoever has too much confidence in himself
Is mistaken, and knows nothing of what he thinks he knows.

I walk with the simple, and open my highest secrets
Only to the truly humble of heart;
To the truly poor in spirit <note>A reference to the Beatitudes: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."</note> I smooth out my decrees,
And unseal the eyes where I see a pure soul.
The curiosity that a vain pride conducts
Makes for itself, out of its false light, an even darker night,
Which hides my clarity all the more from its sight:
The more reason exerts itself, the less it understands;

<sig>Ee 4</sig>

<summary>In this passage, Jesus encourages the believer to ignore the intellectual doubts sown by the devil, explaining that spiritual attacks are actually a sign of a soul's progress in virtue. He calls for a simple, firm faith in the Sacrament of the Eucharist, warning that intellectual pride and human reason only serve to obscure divine truth.</summary>
<keywords>temptation, virtue, faith vs. reason, Holy Sacrament, humility, spiritual pride, divine mystery, poor in spirit</keywords>

--- Page 522 ---
<meta>This page concludes Book IV of 'The Imitation of Jesus Christ,' translated into French verse by the playwright Pierre Corneille. It completes the final discourse on the Holy Sacrament, emphasizing the necessity of prioritizing faith and love over intellectual inquiry.</meta>

<page-num>440</page-num>
<header>THE IMITATION OF JESUS CHRIST</header>

Just as it <note>Referring to human reason, which the previous page established as being prone to error.</note> is weak, it is often deceived,
But solid faith is never mistaken.

All these discernments that Nature <note>In this theological context, "Nature" refers to human natural ability and intellect, as opposed to divine Grace.</note> inspires,
All this research where the senses might guide us,
Must follow the faith they wish to precede,
Must support it, and not destroy it.
It is faith, it is love—both of them triumphant—
In this feast <note>The "feast" refers to the Eucharist, the central theme of Book IV.</note> that God presents to His children,
Who walk side by side, possessing equal strength;
And their holy union, through unknown mechanisms,
Accomplishes all this great work, and all these wonders,
Which surpass every effort of human reasoning.

The sovereign power of this absolute Master,
Which neither time nor place can limit,
Operates a thousand effects on Earth and in the Heavens,
Which man sees and admires, but cannot fully know.
The more the mind labors over them, the more it is confounded;
The deeper it probes, the less it sees the bottom;
They are always obscure, and always admirable:
And if they were understood by reason,
The names of "marvelous" and "ineffable" <note>original: "ineffables"—meaning that which is beyond the power of words to describe.</note>,
However highly they were regarded, would not be their due.

->THE END<-

<summary>This concluding page of The Imitation of Christ asserts that while human reason is fallible and limited, faith and love together allow the believer to experience the divine mysteries of the Eucharist. It ends the work by celebrating the "ineffable" power of God that transcends human understanding.</summary>
<keywords>faith, reason, Eucharist, Pierre Corneille, Thomas à Kempis, divine mystery, love, transcendence</keywords>

<meta>This page follows the conclusion of the Table of Contents for the Fourth Book. It provides the legal authorization for the publication of this specific edition of "The Imitation of Jesus Christ" in verse by the famous French playwright Pierre Corneille.</meta>

# EXTRACT
## OF THE KING'S PRIVILEGE.

Philip, by the grace of God, King of Castile, of Leon, of Aragon, etc. Archduke of Austria, Duke of Burgundy, of Brabant, etc. <note>Philip IV of Spain, who at the time ruled the Spanish Netherlands (modern-day Belgium), where this book was published.</note> Grants to François Foppens the right to be the sole printer of *The Imitation of Jesus Christ* in Verse by Pierre Corneille. And he forbids all Printers, Booksellers, and others from printing it, or from selling it if printed elsewhere or counterfeited, within the term of nine years, under a fine of 30 francs for each Copy, as can be seen more fully in the Letters Patent <note>A "privilege" or "letters patent" was an early form of copyright granted by the monarch to a specific publisher to protect their investment.</note> given at Brussels on December 24, 1663.

->S I G N E D<-

->D E  F R E N.<-

On October 11, 1690, this Privilege was renewed for nine years under the Reign of King Charles II.

->S I G N E D<-

->L O Y E N S.<-

On October 20, 1703, this Privilege was renewed again for nine years under the Reign of King Philip V.

->S I G N E D<-

->L O Y E N S.<-

<summary>This page contains the "Privilege," a legal document granting the printer François Foppens exclusive rights to publish Pierre Corneille's verse translation of "The Imitation of Jesus Christ" and detailing its subsequent renewals.</summary>
<keywords>Royal Privilege, copyright, François Foppens, Pierre Corneille, Brussels, printing history, 17th century publishing, Philip IV, Charles II, Philip V</keywords>
